                                                 SMALL CANCELLATION STABILITY AND ISOMORPHISM RIGIDITY FOR
                                                            GENERIC FINITELY PRESENTED GROUPS


                                                                                                            ILYA KAPOVICH



                                                    Abstract. Let Fm = F (a1 , . . . , am ) with m ≥ 2, and fix q ≥ 1. For every fixed 0 < λ < 1, we prove
                                                    that a q-tuple Wn of independent uniformly random cyclically reduced words of length n is λ-stable with
arXiv:2608.17238v1 [math.GR] 18 Aug 2026




                                                    probability converging to 1 exponentially fast. Namely, for every Φ ∈ Aut(Fm ), the tuple Φ(Wn ), after
                                                    cyclic reduction and symmetrization, satisfies the C ′ (λ) small cancellation condition.
                                                       Combining generic λ-stability with Greendlinger normal-closure rigidity and with previous results of
                                                    Kapovich-Schupp-Shpilrain on generic Nielsen uniqueness and generic Whitehead rigidity we establish, for
                                                    any fixed m ≥ 2, q ≥ 1, isomorphism rigidity for generic m-generator q-relator groups. Thus we show that
                                                    two such generic groups ⟨a1 , . . . , am |r1 , . . . , rq ⟩ and ⟨a1 , . . . , am |s1 , . . . , sq ⟩ are isomorphic if and only if, after
                                                    possibly permuting and inverting the generators a1 , . . . , am , the relator tuples (r1 , . . . , rq ) and (s1 , . . . , sq )
                                                    are the same, up to reordering, cyclic permutations and inverting the relators. Among the applications, we
                                                    obtain a quadratic-time algorithm that generically solves the isomorphism problem for m-generator q-relator
                                                    groups, and show that the number of isomorphism types represented by m-generator q-relator presentations
                                                    with cyclically reduced relators of length n is asymptotic to
                                                                                                      (2m − 1)qn
                                                                                                                   .
                                                                                                     2m+q m! q! nq
                                                        The proof of generic λ-stability relies on the use of geodesic currents and on our deterministic sufficient
                                                    criterion for a q-tuple W in Fm to be λ-stable in terms of the components of W being sufficiently projectively
                                                    close to filling currents.

                                                 1. Introduction

1.1. Uniform automorphic small cancellation. Random and generic phenomena play a central role in
geometric and combinatorial group theory. Gromov’s density and few-relator models initiated the study of
groups with long random relations [Gro87, Gro93]. Several different models of genericity for finitely presented
groups have been studied, see, for example, [Ol92, Cha95, AO96, Oll05], with word-hyperbolicity being a
persistent common feature of these constructions. Random-group methods have also produced striking
applications beyond hyperbolicity. Gromov used a random-group construction based on expander graphs to
produce finitely generated groups which do not admit a uniform embedding into a Hilbert space [Gro03].
Random groups also provide important sources of Kazhdan groups: in particular, for 1/3 < d < 1/2,
a random group in Gromov’s density model at density d has property (T) with probability tending to
one [Zuk03, KK13]. Random groups in the few relator model exhibit other interesting properties, such as
bounded rank local freeness and Nielsen uniqueness, [AO96, Arz97, KS05], with applications to isomorphism
rigidity for random one-relator groups [KSS06, KS09].
    Throughout the paper,
                        Fm = F (A) = F (a1 , . . . , am ),   m ≥ 2,    A = {a1 , . . . , am }.
Whenever Xn is a sequence of nonempty finite sampling spaces, we say that subsets Yn ⊆ Xn are exponentially
generic if there are constants C, c > 0 such that
                                                  |Yn |
                                              1−        ≤ Ce−cn
                                                  |Xn |
for every n ≥ 1. Likewise, a sequence of events En occurs with exponentially high probability if P(En ) ≥
1 − Ce−cn for some C, c > 0 and every n ≥ 1.
   The isomorphism-rigidity theorem of Kapovich-Schupp-Shpilrain for random one-relator groups in [KSS06]
says, roughly, that one-relator groups Gr = ⟨a1 , . . . , am |r⟩ and Gs = ⟨a1 , . . . , am |s⟩, with long ”random”
cyclically reduced defining relator r, s ∈ Fm , are isomorphic as groups if and only if there exists a “relabeling”
automorphism Θ of Fm permuting and possibly inverting the generators A, such that r is a cyclic permutation
of Θ(s±1 ). The proof of this result in [KSS06] combined three main ingredients. First, the Nielsen-uniqueness
theorem of Kapovich–Schupp [KS05] says that, for fixed m ≥ 2 and q ≥ 1, there is an exponentially generic
class of m-generator q-relator presentations whose groups have a single Nielsen class of m-tuples generating
nonfree subgroups. Second, Kapovich–Schupp–Shpilrain [KSS06] gave a generic-case analysis of Whitehead’s
algorithm in Fm : generic cyclically reduced words satisfy a strong Whitehead-minimality condition, and
automorphic equivalence between such words reduces to relabeling and cyclic permutation. Third, Magnus’s
classical normal-closure theorem [Mag30] says that elements r, s ∈ Fm have the same normal closure if and
only if r is conjugate in Fm to s±1 . In the one-relator case, these three inputs turn an abstract group
isomorphism into the explicit relation between relators needed for isomorphism rigidity.
   For q ≥ 2 defining relators, the analogous conclusion of Magnus’s theorem is false for relator sets in
general, and this fact was the main obstacle to extending the results of [KSS06] to random multi-relator
quotients of free groups. Kapovich–Schupp overcame the corresponding difficulty in [KS09] for random q-
relator quotients of the modular group M = Z2 ∗ Z3 . There the finite orders of the standard generators
and the restricted Nielsen theory for generating pairs provide enough additional control to combine small
cancellation with a Greendlinger-type normal-closure argument. The analogous generic multi-relator rigidity
problem for quotients of Fm remained open. In the present paper, we overcome this difficulty by proving
λ-stability for random q-tuples of relators in Fm , for every q ≥ 1, and combining it with Greendlinger’s
theorem [Gre61] for symmetrized small-cancellation sets having the same normal closure. This supplies the
required multi-relator substitute for Magnus’s theorem; the other inputs are the Nielsen-uniqueness results
of [KS05] and the generic Whitehead-minimality and stabilizer results of [KSS06].
   The missing ingredient is therefore a normal-closure uniqueness principle robust enough to survive arbi-
trary automorphisms of Fm . This situation leads naturally to the stability problem studied here: whether
                  ISOMORPHISM RIGIDITY FOR FOR GENERIC FINITELY PRESENTED GROUPS                                3


small cancellation holds uniformly throughout the automorphic orbit of a random relator tuple. The order
of quantifiers is crucially important. For any fixed Φ ∈ Aut(Fm ) standard quasi-isometry considerations
imply that, for any fixed 0 < λ < 1, there exists 0 < λ′ < λ such that a sufficiently long cyclically reduced
C ′ (λ′ )-word w ∈ Fm has the property that the cyclic reduction of Φ(w) satisfies C ′ (λ), after symmetrization.
Since for any 0 < λ′ < 1, random cyclically reduced wn ∈ Fm satisfy C ′ (λ′ ) for all large enough n, it follows
that the cyclic reduction of Φ(wn ) satisfies C ′ (λ), after symmetrization. However, requiring that a random
cyclically reduced word satisfies this conclusion for all Φ ∈ Aut(Fm ) makes the problem much more difficult.
   For g ̸= 1, let ∥g∥A be the cyclically reduced length of its conjugacy class. Recall informally that a
nontrivial element is root-free if it is not a proper power, and a tuple is root-free if each of its entries is
root-free; a tuple is irredundant if no two distinct entries are conjugate to one another, even after inverting
one of them.
   In this paper we introduce and study the following new key notion. For 0 < λ < 1, we call a tuple of
cyclically reduced words in Fm λ-stable if, after applying any automorphism of Fm and cyclically reducing,
its symmetrization satisfies C ′ (λ). See Subsection 2.1 for the precise definitions.
Remark 1.1 (Small cancellation versus stability). Ordinary C ′ (λ) small cancellation is far weaker than λ-
stability. If m ≥ 3, 0 < λ ≤ 1/6, and Wn is a uniform positive word of length n in F (a2 , . . . , am ),
then a1 Wn satisfies C ′ (λ) with exponentially high probability but is primitive, hence not λ-stable. Indeed,
                                                                                                   ′
the automorphic orbit of every primitive element contains a1 aN  2 , whose symmetrization fails C (λ) for all
sufficiently large N . The phenomenon already occurs in rank two: the positive word
                                              a5 ba3 b2 ababa2 b4 ab3
has length 25, is root-free, and satisfies C ′ (1/6), but its image under a 7→ ab, b 7→ b has two distinct cyclic
conjugates with common prefix (ab)4 of length 8 > 38/6.

   For a root-free irredundant tuple g = (g1 , . . . , gq ), let ∆A (g) denote its supremal automorphic piece
ratio. For each φ ∈ Out(Fm ), choose an automorphism representing φ, cyclically reduce the images of
the components of g, and symmetrize the resulting tuple by taking all cyclic shifts of these words and their
inverses. For every ordered pair of distinct words r, r′ in this symmetrization, let v be their maximal common
initial segment and record the ratio
                                                       |v|A
                                                            .
                                                       |r|A
Then ∆A (g) is the supremum of these ratios over all such ordered pairs and all φ ∈ Out(Fm ), with value 0
when no pieces occur; if g is not root-free and irredundant, we put ∆A (g) = ∞. Thus ∆A (g) measures the
worst relative piece overlap occurring anywhere in the automorphic orbit of g, and ∆A (g) < λ implies that
g is λ-stable. See Definition 3.2 for the formal definition.
   For n ≥ 1, let Cn and Fn be the sets of cyclically and freely reduced words of length n over A±1 ,
respectively. Unless stated otherwise, random choices are uniform. For a positive sequence an , we write
Yn = OP (an ) if Yn /an is bounded in probability; explicitly, for every δ > 0 there is K > 0 such that
P(|Yn | > Kan ) < δ for all sufficiently large n.

  The deterministic core underlying these probabilistic conclusions is a finite-frequency criterion. For a
nontrivial freely reduced word v and a nontrivial cyclically reduced word W , let (v, W )A be the number of
nonsymmetrized cyclic occurrences of v in W , and put
                                 ⟨v, W ⟩A = (v, W )A + (v −1 , W )A = (v ±1 , W )A .
Let TA be the unit-edge Cayley tree of Fm with respect to A, and let ∂Fm be its Gromov boundary. A
geodesic current on Fm is a positive locally finite Borel measure on ∂ 2 Fm = (∂Fm × ∂Fm ) \ {(ξ, ξ)} that is
invariant under the diagonal Fm -action and the flip (ξ, ζ) 7→ (ζ, ξ). For such a current ν and a nontrivial
freely reduced word v, the cylinder coordinate ⟨v, ν⟩A is the ν-mass of the set of oriented geodesics in TA
containing the oriented segment [1, v]. The counting current ηW associated to a nontrivial cyclically reduced
word W is characterized by ⟨v, ηW ⟩A = ⟨v, W ⟩A . The standard tree–current intersection form is denoted
⟨T, ν⟩; the current ν is filling if this quantity is positive for every nontrivial tree T ∈ cvm , the length-function
closure of Outer space. These notions are recalled in detail in Subsections 2.2–2.3.
Theorem 1.3 (Finite-frequency stability criterion). Fix q ≥ 1 and let ν1 , . . . , νq be filling geodesic currents
on Fm satisfying
                                       ⟨TA , νi ⟩ = 1   (1 ≤ i ≤ q),
and let 0 < λ < 1. Then there exist constants 0 < ε < 1 and 0 < λ′ < λ, and integers M, n0 ≥ 1, such that
the following holds. Let
                                            W = (W1 , . . . , Wq )
                  ISOMORPHISM RIGIDITY FOR FOR GENERIC FINITELY PRESENTED GROUPS                                5


be a root-free irredundant tuple of nontrivial cyclically reduced words, not necessarily of equal lengths, and
put
                                     ℓi = ∥Wi ∥A = |Wi |A      (1 ≤ i ≤ q).
Suppose that ℓi ≥ n0 for every i, that the symmetrization of W satisfies C ′ (λ′ ), and that, for every 1 ≤ i ≤ q
and every nontrivial freely reduced word v with |v|A ≤ M ,
                                            ⟨v, Wi ⟩A
                                                      − ⟨v, νi ⟩A < ε.
                                                ℓi
Then
                                                 ∆A (W) < λ.
In particular, W is λ-stable.

   Thus, for root-free irredundant tuples, a property quantified over all automorphisms of Fm follows from
ordinary small cancellation together with finitely many local frequency inequalities normalized by the indi-
vidual relator lengths. Theorem 1.3 is proved in Section 4.
   We prove Theorem A in Section 5, followed by a restatement and proof of Corollary 1.2. Theorem A serves
as the main tool to establish subsequent probabilistic results. The proof of Theorem A combines geometric
arguments regarding Outer space, bounded backtracking and optimal Lipschitz distortion with arguments
involving geodesic currents and the Kapovich-Lustig intersection form [KL09, KL10].
   Proposition 3.10 provides a key deterministic bound on the length of a piece v for the symmetrized closure
of φ(W), where W is an arbitrary irredundant root-free q-tuple of cyclically reduced words in Fm :
                                       |v| ≤ 2ΛA (φ) ρ±
                                                                   
                                                      per (W) + 2m .

Here ρ±per (W) records a geometrically defined upper bound for the maximum piece length for the symmetriza-
tion of (the cyclically reduced form of) W, and ΛA (φ) is the optimal Lipschitz constant of an Fm -equivariant
map TA → TA φ, where TA is the Cayley tree of Fm = F (A) with respect to A. Lemma lem:uniform-filling-
neighborhood shows that for a suitably chosen neigborhood U of a filling current ν, every current η ∈ U has
a controlled distortion under the action of arbitrary φ ∈ Out(Fm ), namely
                                              ⟨TA , φη⟩ ≥ cΛA (φ)
where c > 0 is some constant independent of φ and η. In particular, this inequality applies to “rational”
currents in U corresponding to conjugacy classes in Fm . Combining these tools ultimately allows us to
deduce Theorem 1.3.
   Section 4 first proves the deterministic finite-frequency criterion and then derives the probabilistic master
estimate from finite-coordinate concentration and signed-overlap tails. Section 6 then recovers λ-stability
for independent positive Bernoulli words, allowing different strictly positive probability vectors among com-
ponents, and records an almost-sure extension to finitely supported group random walks; see Corollary 6.4.

1.2. Generic multi-relator rigidity. The preceding stability theorem, combined with Greendlinger’s
normal-closure theorem and the Nielsen and Whitehead inputs described above, yields the generic multi-
relator rigidity theorem. Let Rel(A) denote the finite group of signed relabeling automorphisms of Fm , that
is, automorphisms that permute A±1 and commute with inversion. Thus
                                               | Rel(A)| = 2m m!.
Theorem B (Generic few-relator rigidity). Fix m ≥ 2 and q ≥ 1. For a finite tuple R = (r1 , . . . , rs ) of
elements of Fm , write
                                          GR = ⟨a1 , . . . , am | r1 , . . . , rs ⟩,
and denote by ai the image of ai in GR . Here and below, “finitely specified” means that, for fixed m, q, finite
rational auxiliary data are chosen once and for all; no uniform procedure producing these data from m and
q is asserted. There are finitely specified subsets
                                          Qm,q (n) ⊆ Cnq      (n ≥ 1)
6                                                     I. KAPOVICH


and constants C, c > 0 such that:
(1) For every n ≥ 1, a uniform random tuple in Cnq belongs to Qm,q (n) with probability at least 1 − Ce−cn .
    Membership in Qm,q (n) is decidable in deterministic polynomial time in n.
(2) Every q-tuple R ∈ Qm,q (n) is irredundant, root-free, and 1/6-stable.
(3) If R = (r1 , . . . , rq ) ∈ Qm,q (n), then GR is torsion-free, one-ended, and non-elementary hyperbolic; every
    subgroup generated by at most m − 1 elements is free; every m-tuple generating a nonfree subgroup is
    Nielsen-equivalent to the standard tuple (a1 , . . . , am ); and GR is co-Hopfian, meaning that every injective
    endomorphism of GR is surjective.
(4) If R = (r1 , . . . , rq ) ∈ Qm,q (n), then GR is complete, meaning that its center is trivial and every auto-
    morphism of GR is inner. Its boundary is one-dimensional, connected, and has no local cut points, and
    hence is homeomorphic to the Menger curve or the Sierpiński carpet. If q ≥ m − 1, then ∂GR is the
    Menger curve.
(5) Let R = (r1 , . . . , rq ) ∈ Qm,q (n), and let S = (s1 , . . . , st ) be an irredundant tuple of nontrivial elements
    of Fm whose symmetrization of cyclically reduced representatives satisfies C ′ (1/6). Then GR ∼             = GS if
    and only if t = q and there are Φ ∈ Aut(Fm ), σ ∈ Sym(q), signs εi ∈ {±1}, and gi ∈ Fm such that
                                        Φ(ri ) = gi sεσ(i)
                                                       i
                                                           gi−1      (1 ≤ i ≤ q).
                                                                                          ∼ GS if and only if n = n′ and
(6) If R = (r1 , . . . , rq ) ∈ Qm,q (n) and S = (s1 , . . . , sq ) ∈ Qm,q (n′ ), then GR =
    there are Θ ∈ Rel(A), σ ∈ Sym(q), and signs εi ∈ {±1} such that, for each i = 1, . . . , q, the word si is
    a cyclic permutation of Θ(rσ(i) )εi .
Remark 1.4 (Stability Conjecture). The Stability Conjecture of Kapovich–Schupp [KS05b, Conjecture 1.2]
says the following. Fix m ≥ 2 and q ≥ 1. There exists an algorithmically recognizable generic family
Dn ⊆ Cnq , n ≥ 1, with the following property. If σ ∈ Dn , τ ∈ Dnq ′ and Φ ∈ Aut(Fm ) satisfy
                                                NRA (σ) = NRA (Φ(τ )) ,
then
                                             RA (σ) = RA (Φ(τ )).
Theorem B directly gives this conclusion in the present few-relator model, in an exponentially generic and
polynomial-time recognizable form. Indeed, part (1) gives the exponentially generic recognizable classes
Qm,q (n), while part (2) says that every tuple in these classes is irredundant, root-free, and 1/6-stable. Thus,
if
                                       σ ∈ Qm,q (n),       τ ∈ Qm,q (n′ )
for some n, n′ ≥ 1 and Φ ∈ Aut(Fm ), then both RA (σ) and RA (Φ(τ )) satisfy C ′ (1/6). If these two
symmetrized sets have the same normal closure, Theorem 8.2 gives their equality. Hence Theorem B directly
implies the Stability Conjecture (in fact with exponential genericity in the model used here).
Remark 1.5 (Labelled Cayley graphs). Part (6) has the following equivalent labelled-graph formulation. If
                                          R ∈ Qm,q (n),           S ∈ Qm,q (n′ ),
then GR ∼
        = GS if and only if there are Θ ∈ Rel(A) and a graph isomorphism
                                            Cay(GR , A) −→ Cay(GS , A)
that sends every oriented edge labelled a ∈ A±1 to an oriented edge labelled Θ(a). Equivalently, after
relabelling the edge labels of the target Cayley graph by Θ−1 , the two Cayley graphs are isomorphic as
A±1 -labelled graphs.

    Section 10 proves Theorem B, using the Greendlinger normal-closure theorem from Section 8.

1.3. Algorithms and enumeration. The same rigidity description yields efficient isomorphism procedures
on the generic class and an asymptotic enumeration of the resulting isomorphism types.
Theorem C (Isomorphism algorithms). Fix m ≥ 2 and q ≥ 1. For a finite tuple U = (u1 , . . . , us ) of
elements of Fm , write
                                GU = ⟨a1 , . . . , am | u1 , . . . , us ⟩.
(1) Fix R = (r1 , . . . , rq ) ∈ Qm,q (n0 ). There is a quadratic-time algorithm for the following restricted iso-
    morphism problem. The input is a finite tuple S = (s1 , . . . , st ) of nontrivial cyclically reduced words
    known to be irredundant and to have symmetrization satisfying C ′ (1/6); the algorithm decides whether
    GR ∼= GS . With
                                                         Xt
                                                    N=      |sj |A ,
                                                              j=1
    the running time is O(N ). (The assumption on S can be checked within the same O(N 2 ) bound; an
                                 2

    input failing it is reported as outside the restricted problem.)
(2) There is a linear-time algorithm which, given tuples R ∈ Cnq and S ∈ Cnq ′ known to belong to Qm,q (n) and
    Qm,q (n′ ), respectively, decides whether GR ∼= GS . The algorithm’s running time is linear in max{n, n′ }.
    The algorithm does not test the assumptions on R, S.

   We prove Theorem C in Subsection 11.1.

Theorem D (Asymptotic number of isomorphism types). Fix m ≥ 2 and q ≥ 1. For n ≥ 1 let Im,q (n) be
the number of group isomorphism types represented by presentations
                                               ⟨a1 , . . . , am | r1 , . . . , rq ⟩,
where r1 , . . . , rq are cyclically reduced words of length n in Fm = F (a1 , . . . , am ). Then
                                        cr           (2m − 1)qn
                                       Im,q (n) ∼                               (n → ∞).
                                                    2m+q m! q! nq

  Here ∼ means that the ratio of the two quantities goes to 1 as n → ∞. We prove Theorem D in
Subsection 11.2. For q = 1, the conclusion of Theorem D agrees with the precise one-relator asymptotic of
Kapovich–Schupp [KS05b].

1.4. Organization. Section 2 gives the preliminaries. Sections 3–4 establish the deterministic overlap esti-
mate, the finite-frequency stability criterion, and its probabilistic consequences. Section 5 proves Theorem A
and Corollary 1.2, and Section 6 treats positive Bernoulli words and records an almost-sure extension to
finitely supported group random walks. Section 7 records the Nielsen and Whitehead inputs. Section 8
proves normal-closure rigidity. Sections 9–10 prove Theorem B, and Section 11 gives the algorithms and
enumeration.

                                                  2. Preliminaries

   We collect notation and standard facts used below.

2.1. Free groups, cyclic words, and small cancellation.
Convention 2.1 (Standing free-group notation). Unless explicitly stated otherwise, m ≥ 2, Fm = F (A) is
the free group with fixed basis
                                               A = {a1 , . . . , am },
and TA is its unit-edge Cayley tree. We identify elements of Fm with their freely reduced words over A±1 .
For u ∈ Fm , let |u|A be its freely reduced length, [u] its conjugacy class, and ∥u∥A the cyclically reduced
length of [u], equivalently the translation length of u in TA . Subscripts are omitted when the basis is clear.
8                                                 I. KAPOVICH


A positive word is a word over A, and An denotes the set of positive words of length n. This convention
remains in force throughout the paper unless explicitly overridden.
Definition 2.2 (Root-free and irredundant tuples). (1) A nontrivial element g ∈ Fm is root-free if it is not
    a proper power.
(2) A tuple (s1 , . . . , st ) of nontrivial elements of Fm is root-free if every entry is root-free.
(3) A tuple of nontrivial elements of Fm is irredundant if no two distinct entries are conjugate to one another
    or to one another’s inverses.

    For a set R of nontrivial cyclically reduced words in Fm , its symmetrization R consists of all cyclic
permutations of elements of R±1 ; and such a set R is symmetrized if R = R. A nonempty word v is a piece
of a symmetrized set R if it is a common initial segment of two distinct elements of R. The set R satisfies
C ′ (λ) if every piece v beginning r ∈ R satisfies
                                                  |v| < λ|r|A .
Let g = (g1 , . . . , gq ) be a tuple of nontrivial elements of Fm , and choose cyclically reduced representatives
ui ∈ [gi ]. We denote by RA (g) the symmetrization of the set {u1 , . . . , uq }. These conventions are consistent
with the standard small-cancellation terminology of [LS77, Chapter V].
   For φ ∈ Out(Fm ), define RA (φ(g)) := RA (Φ(g)) and ∥φ(gi )∥A := ∥Φ(gi )∥A using any representative
Φ ∈ Aut(Fm ) of the outer automorphism φ. These notations are well defined because inner automorphisms
preserve conjugacy classes.
Definition 2.3 (λ-stability). Let 0 < λ < 1.
(1) A set R ⊆ Fm \ {1} is λ-stable if, for every Φ ∈ Aut(Fm ), the symmetrization of cyclically reduced forms
    of the elements of Φ(R) satisfies C ′ (λ).
(2) A tuple is λ-stable if its underlying set is λ-stable.
(3) A nontrivial element is λ-stable if its singleton set is λ-stable.

   Let v be a nontrivial freely reduced word over A±1 and w = x0 · · · xℓ−1 a nontrivial cyclically reduced
word of length ℓ. Put                     
                            (v, w)A := # s ∈ Z/ℓZ : xs xs+1 · · · xs+|v|A −1 = v ,
where subscripts are read modulo ℓ. Thus (v, w)A is the number of nonsymmetrized cyclic occurrences of v
in w. Put
                                 ⟨v, w⟩A := (v, w)A + (v −1 , w)A = (v ±1 , w)A .
Thus ⟨v, w⟩A is the corresponding symmetrized cyclic occurrence count; the notation (v ±1 , w)A is shorthand
for the displayed sum. Both quantities depend only on the cyclic word represented by w.
    For later counting, the number of freely reduced words of length n ≥ 1 is
                                            |Fn | = 2m(2m − 1)n−1 .
The number of cyclically reduced words is
                                    |Cn | = (2m − 1)n + m + (m − 1)(−1)n .                                    (1)
                                                          ±1
Indeed, |Cn | is the trace of the adjacency matrix on A in which a letter may be followed by every letter
except its inverse; that matrix has eigenvalues 2m − 1, 1 with multiplicity m, and −1 with multiplicity m − 1.
   A signed relabeling automorphism, or simply a relabeling automorphism, is an automorphism induced by
a permutation of A±1 commuting with inversion. The finite group of such automorphisms is denoted Rel(A)
and has order
                                            | Rel(A)| = 2m m!.
                  ISOMORPHISM RIGIDITY FOR FOR GENERIC FINITELY PRESENTED GROUPS                              9


2.2. Trees and Outer space. We use Culler–Vogtmann Outer space and its length-function compactifica-
tion [CV86, CM87, CL95, Gui00, LL03, FM11]. Let cvm be the space, up to equivariant isometry, of free,
minimal, discrete simplicial metric Fm -trees with finite quotient, and let cvm be its length-function closure.
Its nonzero points are nontrivial minimal very small trees: tripod stabilizers are trivial and nondegenerate
arc stabilizers are trivial or maximal cyclic; see also [GL07, Gui08]. For T ∈ cvm and g ∈ Fm , let
                                             ∥g∥T := inf dT (x, gx)
                                                      x∈T

be the translation length. If T is free and simplicial and g ̸= 1, then g has an axis, denoted AT (g).
  We use the standard right action of Out(Fm ) on cvm , denoted T φ, and characterized by
                          ∥g∥T φ = ∥φ(g)∥T       (T ∈ cvm , φ ∈ Out(Fm ), g ∈ Fm ).
Thus TA φ is the pullback of TA by φ; it may be represented by the same underlying metric tree as TA , with
the Fm -action precomposed by any automorphism representing φ. In particular,
                                              ∥g∥TA φ = ∥φ(g)∥A .
Definition 2.4 (Lipschitz factor and normalized slice). Let T ∈ cvm \ {0}.
(1) The A-Lipschitz factor of T is
                            ΛA (T ) := inf{Lip(f ) : f : TA → T is Fm -equivariant}.
(2) The corresponding normalized slice is
                                       KA := {T ∈ cvm : ΛA (T ) = 1}.
(3) For φ ∈ Out(Fm ), put
                                             ΛA (φ) := ΛA (TA φ).

   The definition of ΛA (T ) has a concrete displacement interpretation. An Fm -equivariant map f : TA → T
is determined, after straightening the images of edges to geodesic segments, by the image x = f (1) of the
identity vertex. Since every edge of TA /Fm has length one, the straightened map has Lipschitz constant
                                                max dT (x, ax).
                                                a∈A
Consequently,
                                         ΛA (T ) = inf max dT (x, ax).                                     (2)
                                                   x∈T a∈A

   For φ ∈ Out(Fm ), the tree TA φ lies in cvm . Passing to quotient marked graphs identifies an equivari-
ant map TA → TA φ with a change-of-marking map between roses. In the terminology of Francaviglia–
Martino [FM11, Definition 3.7], such a piecewise-linear map is optimal if at every vertex of its maximally
stretched subgraph there is a legal turn, equivalently, the incident maximally stretched edge germs are not
all mapped into one common direction. They prove that optimal maps exist and that the stretching factor
of every optimal map realizes the minimal Lipschitz constant [FM11, Proposition 3.11]. Thus an equivariant
optimal map f : TA → TA φ may be chosen with
                                               Lip(f ) = ΛA (φ).
Proposition 2.5 (Outer-space facts). The following hold.
(1) The projectivized compactification Pcvm is compact.
(2) The function ΛA is positive, continuous, and homogeneous on cvm \ {0}, and KA is compact.

Proof. Culler–Morgan compactness [CM87, Theorem 4.5] gives part (1); see also [CL95, Gui00, LL03]. Ho-
mogeneity of (2) is immediate, and continuity in the length-function topology is standard [CM87, FM11];
compare [GL07, Gui08]. For positivity, if ΛA (T ) = 0, choose xk ∈ T with maxa∈A dT (xk , axk ) → 0. The
displacement of each word at xk is bounded by its word length times this maximum, so every g ∈ Fm is
elliptic. A finitely generated group acting on an R-tree with every element elliptic has a global fixed point,
10                                                  I. KAPOVICH


contradicting nontrivial minimality. Thus every projective class has a unique representative with ΛA (T ) = 1,
and
                                                         T
                                              [T ] 7−→
                                                       ΛA (T )
is a homeomorphism Pcvm → KA , so KA is compact.                                                            □

   There is also a useful finite description of the quantity in Definition 2.4. Proposition 3.15 of [FM11] says
that the maximal stretching between two marked metric graphs is realized by a candidate loop. When the
source is the standard rose TA /Fm , the candidates are represented by cyclically reduced words of A-length
at most two. Hence, for T ∈ cvm ,
                                                                                    
                                           ∥u∥T
                         ΛA (T ) = max           : u cyclically reduced, 1 ≤ |u|A ≤ 2 .                     (3)
                                           |u|A
Thus ΛA (T ) is determined by the translation lengths ∥u∥T of freely reduced words u with 1 ≤ |u|A ≤ 2.
Since cvm is dense in cvm , the left-hand side of (3) is continuous by Proposition 2.5, and the right-hand side
is a finite maximum of translation-length coordinates, the same formula holds for every nontrivial T ∈ cvm .
  If T, T ′ are free, minimal, cocompact simplicial Fm -trees and f : T → T ′ is an Fm -equivariant Lipschitz
map, its bounded-backtracking constant is
                            BBT(f ) = sup{dT ′ (f (z), [f (x), f (y)]) : z ∈ [x, y]}.
The map f map is a quasi-isometry, hence induces ∂T =   ∼ ∂T ′ . The following key facts records a particularly
useful BBT (f ) estimate [BFH97, Lemma 3.1]:
Proposition 2.6 (BBT bound). Let T, T ′ ∈ cvm (where m ≥ 2) and let f : T → T ′ be an Fm -equivariant
Lipschitz map.
                                         BBT(f ) ≤ Lip(f ) vol(T /Fm ),                           (4)
where vol(T /Fm ) is the total edge length of the quotient graph.

     In particular, an equivariant K-Lipschitz map TA → T ′ has bounded-backtracking constant at most mK.

2.3. Geodesic currents and the intersection form. Let ∂Fm be the Gromov boundary of Fm and put
                                   ∂ 2 Fm = (∂Fm × ∂Fm ) \ {(ξ, ξ) : ξ ∈ ∂Fm }.
Let ι : ∂ 2 Fm → ∂ 2 Fm be the flip ι(ξ, ζ) = (ζ, ξ). We identify ∂ 2 Fm with the space of oriented bi-infinite
geodesics in TA . A geodesic current on Fm is a positive locally finite Borel measure on ∂ 2 Fm invariant under
the diagonal action of Fm and under ι; see [KL09, KL10]. Write Curr(Fm ) for the space of geodesic currents
and
                                    P Curr(Fm ) := (Curr(Fm ) \ {0})/R>0 .
We equip Curr(Fm ) with the weak-∗ topology.
     For ν ∈ Curr(Fm ), its support is
                     supp(ν) = {z ∈ ∂ 2 Fm : ν(U ) > 0 for every open neighborhood U ∋ z}.
It is a closed Fm - and ι-invariant subset of ∂ 2 Fm . The boundary action of Aut(Fm ) induces an Out(Fm )-
action on currents, since inner automorphisms act trivially on Fm -invariant measures, and
                                                         
                                 supp(φν) = φ supp(ν)         (φ ∈ Out(Fm )).
Our action conventions give φηg = ηφ(g) and
                            ⟨TA , φη⟩ = ⟨TA φ, η⟩      (η ∈ Curr(Fm ), φ ∈ Out(Fm )).                      (5)
Positive rescaling does not change support.
     For 1 ̸= g ∈ Fm , let g +∞ , g −∞ ∈ ∂Fm be its attracting and repelling fixed points and put
                                            ℓg = (g −∞ , g +∞ ) ∈ ∂ 2 Fm .
                   ISOMORPHISM RIGIDITY FOR FOR GENERIC FINITELY PRESENTED GROUPS                                 11


The elements of Fm · ℓg ∪ Fm · ι(ℓg ) are the periodic leaves associated to [g]. If ηg is the counting current of
[g], then
                                        supp(ηg ) = Fm · ℓg ∪ Fm · ι(ℓg ).
For a nontrivial freely reduced word v, let CylA (v) ⊆ ∂ 2 Fm be the cylinder of oriented geodesics containing
the oriented segment [1, v] ⊆ TA , and put
                                                                  
                                            ⟨v, ν⟩A := ν CylA (v) .
For a nontrivial cyclically reduced word w, the cyclic-occurrence notation from Section 2.1 satisfies
                                               ⟨v, ηw ⟩A = ⟨v, w⟩A .
The cylinder coordinates determine the weak-∗ topology on Curr(Fm ): for every ν ∈ Curr(Fm ), neighbor-
hoods specified by finitely many inequalities
                                             |⟨v, η⟩A − ⟨v, ν⟩A | < εv
with nontrivial freely reduced words v and constants εv > 0 form a neighborhood basis at ν.
  The geometric intersection form
                                        ⟨·, ·⟩ : cvm × Curr(Fm ) −→ R≥0
is continuous and satisfies
                                             ⟨T, ηg ⟩ = ∥g∥T .
A nonzero current ν is filling in Curr(Fm ) if ⟨T, ν⟩ > 0 for every nontrivial T ∈ cvm . For boundary
trees, dual laminations, and currents, see [CHL08a, CHL08b, CHL08c]. We use the following standard
facts [CM87, KL09, KL10, KL15].
Proposition 2.7 (Current facts). The following hold.
(1) The intersection form is continuous, homogeneous in the tree coordinate, and linear in the current
    coordinate.
(2) For every φ ∈ Out(Fm ), T ∈ cvm , ν ∈ Curr(Fm ) we have
                                                ⟨T φ, ν⟩ = ⟨T, φν⟩.
(3) For T ∈ cvm \ {0} and ν ∈ Curr(Fm ),
                                     ⟨T, ν⟩ = 0    ⇐⇒      supp(ν) ⊆ L2 (T ),
    where L2 (T ) ⊆ ∂ 2 Fm is the dual algebraic lamination of T ; this is the zero-intersection criterion
    of [KL10, Theorem 1.1].

                         3. Signed periodic overlaps and automorphic pieces

  We identify signed periodic overlaps with intersections of translates of relator axes.
Lemma 3.1 (Uniqueness of symmetrized representatives). Let g = (g1 , . . . , gq ) be a root-free irredundant
tuple of nontrivial elements of Fm , and choose cyclically reduced representatives ui of [gi ]. If a cyclic shift of
uεi equals a cyclic shift of uδj , where ε, δ ∈ {±1}, then i = j, ε = δ, and the starting positions agree modulo
|ui |. Thus every member of RA (g) has a unique origin triple consisting of a component, an orientation, and
a cyclic position.

Proof. If i ̸= j, equality makes gi conjugate to gj±1 , contrary to irredundancy. If i = j and ε = δ, distinct
starting positions give a nontrivial cyclic period, contrary to root-freeness. Finally, no nontrivial free-group
element is conjugate to its inverse. If hgh−1 = g −1 , then h2 centralizes g. If h2 = 1, torsion-freeness
gives h = 1 and g = g −1 ; if h2 ̸= 1, then g, h lie in the cyclic centralizer of h2 and commute. Both are
impossible.                                                                                                    □
12                                                   I. KAPOVICH


Definition 3.2 (Admissibility and automorphic piece ratio). A tuple g = (g1 , . . . , gq ) of nontrivial elements
of Fm is admissible if it is root-free and irredundant.
     For an admissible tuple define
                                                                                   
                                                   |v| r ∈ RA (φ(g)),              
                       ∆A (g) =   sup      sup        : v is a piece of RA (φ(g))     ,
                                φ∈Out(Fm )      |r|A
                                                        and an initial segment of r
                                                                                    

where the inner supremum is zero when there are no pieces. If g is not admissible, put ∆A (g) = ∞.

     Admissibility is invariant under automorphisms, and
                               ∆A (g) < λ      =⇒      g is admissible and λ-stable.                                (6)

     Let
                                  w = (w1 , . . . , wq ), wi = xi,0 · · · xi,ℓi −1
be a tuple of nontrivial cyclically reduced words. Indices in the i-th component are read modulo ℓi . For
s ∈ Z/ℓi Z, ε ∈ {+, −}, and r ∈ Z, put
                                   ωi,+,s (r) = xi,s+r ,        ωi,−,s (r) = x−1
                                                                              i,s−r−1 .

Thus ωi,+,s is a cyclic shift of the bi-infinite periodic word wi∞ , while ωi,−,s is a cyclic shift of (wi−1 )∞ .
Definition 3.3 (Signed periodic-overlap length). For a tuple w of nontrivial cyclically reduced words, with
signed periodic words ωi,ε,s as above, define ρ± per (w) as follows. It is 0 if no distinct signed origins exist,
∞ if two distinct signed periodic words agree identically, and otherwise the largest integer R ≥ 0 for which
distinct signed origins satisfy
                                         ωi,ε,s [0, R) = ωj,δ,t [0, R),
where ω[0, R) denotes the word ω(0)ω(1) · · · ω(R − 1), with the empty-word convention when R = 0.
Lemma 3.4 (Infinite signed overlap). Let w be a tuple of nontrivial cyclically reduced words. Then
                                      ρ±
                                       per (w) < ∞         ⇐⇒     w is admissible.

Proof. Identical same-orientation shifts of one component give a nontrivial cyclic period, hence a proper
power. Identical shifts from distinct components make their cyclic words, up to conjugacy and inversion,
powers of a common primitive cyclic word. An exponent of absolute value greater than one violates root-
freeness; if both exponents have absolute value one, irredundancy fails. Identical opposite-orientation shifts
of one component would make the element conjugate to its inverse, impossible by Lemma 3.1. Thus infinite
overlap implies nonadmissibility. Conversely, a proper power yields identical same-orientation shifts, and
conjugate-up-to-inversion components yield identical signed periodic words after suitable shifts.           □
Lemma 3.5 (Pieces and signed periodic overlaps). Let w = (w1 , . . . , wq ) be an admissible tuple of nontrivial
cyclically reduced words. Let
                                   PA (w) = max{|v| : v is a piece of RA (w)},
where PA (w) = 0 if RA (w) has no pieces. Then:
(1)
                                                 PA (w) ≤ ρ±
                                                           per (w).
(2) If |wi |A = n for every 1 ≤ i ≤ q, then
                                                 PA (w) = ρ±
                                                           per (w).
                    ISOMORPHISM RIGIDITY FOR FOR GENERIC FINITELY PRESENTED GROUPS                                    13


Proof. Let v be a piece of RA (w). Thus v is a common initial segment of two distinct members of RA (w).
By Lemma 3.1, these two members have distinct signed origins. Their corresponding signed periodic words
therefore have a common initial segment of length |v|, and hence |v| ≤ ρ±
                                                                        per (w). This proves part (1).

   Suppose now that |wi |A = n for every i. By admissibility and Lemma 3.4, ρ±
                                                                             per (w) < ∞. Moreover,

                                                     ρ±
                                                      per (w) < n.
Indeed, if two distinct signed origins had a common periodic prefix of length at least n, then the corresponding
signed periodic words, both n-periodic, would agree identically, contrary to admissibility. Choose distinct
signed origins realizing ρ±per (w). Since this overlap has length less than n, it is also a common initial segment
of the corresponding two length-n members of RA (w), which are distinct by Lemma 3.1. Thus it is a piece,
so
                                                 PA (w) ≥ ρ± per (w).
Together with part (1), this proves part (2).                                                                   □
Example 3.6 (Strict inequality in Lemma 3.5). Let F2 = F (a, b) and
                                                    w = (ab, aba).
The tuple w is admissible. The signed periodic words
                                   (ab)∞ = ababab · · · ,      (aba)∞ = abaaba · · ·
have common initial segment aba of length 3, and a direct check of the finitely many signed origins shows
that no longer common prefix occurs. Thus
                                                     ρ±
                                                      per (w) = 3.

On the other hand, ab is a piece of RA (w), while no piece has length greater than 2; hence
                                             PA (w) = 2 < 3 = ρ±
                                                               per (w).
The strict inequality occurs because the periodic overlap continues past the end of the shorter relator ab.

  Let T be a free simplicial Fm -tree. For g ̸= 1, let AT (g) be its axis. For an admissible tuple g = (g1 , . . . , gq )
put
                                          OvT (g) = sup diam(ℓ ∩ ℓ′ ),
where the supremum ranges over distinct lines
                                 ℓ = hAT (gi ),      ℓ′ = h′ AT (gj ),     h, h′ ∈ Fm .
The diameter of the empty set is zero.
Lemma 3.7 (Pieces and intersections of axes). Let g be an admissible tuple of nontrivial cyclically reduced
words. Every piece v of RA (g) determines two distinct translates of component axes whose intersection
contains a segment of length |v|. Consequently,
                                                    |v| ≤ OvTA (g).

Proof. Let distinct r, r′ ∈ RA (g) have common initial segment v. By Lemma 3.1, they have distinct
component-orientation-position triples, each determining an oriented fundamental segment on a component-
axis translate. Translating the common initial vertex to the identity makes the two copies of v a common
segment of these translates.
   The underlying lines in TA are distinct. Otherwise their preferred orientations agree, since opposite
orientations cannot read a nonempty common word. Their common line Fm -stabilizer is generated by the
primitive root of either component, forcing distinct components to be conjugate up to inversion or, for one
component, root-freeness to make the triples equal.                                                      □
14                                                   I. KAPOVICH


Lemma 3.8 (Signed periodic factors are axis overlaps). Let w be an admissible tuple of nontrivial cyclically
reduced words. Then
                                         OvTA (w) = ρ± per (w).

Proof. For the i-th component and s ∈ Z/ℓi Z, put
                                        pi,s = xi,0 · · · xi,s−1 ,   pi,0 = 1.
The line p−1
          i,s ATA (wi ) passes through the identity. In its positive translation direction its forward label is the
one-sided restriction of ωi,+,s ; in the opposite direction its forward label is the one-sided restriction of ωi,−,s .
   A common signed periodic factor of length R therefore gives an axis intersection of length R. For R > 0
the lines are distinct: otherwise their agreeing orientations and first common edge force the complete signed
periodic words to agree, contrary to admissibility. Hence
                                                OvTA (w) ≥ ρ±
                                                            per (w).

   Conversely, orient two distinct component-axis translates compatibly on a nondegenerate intersection
and translate its initial vertex to the identity. The oriented lines determine distinct signed origins, and the
intersection reads a common prefix of their periodic words. An unbounded intersection would give a common
ray and, by periodicity, identical signed periodic words, contrary to admissibility. Thus its length is at most
ρ±
 per (w).                                                                                                    □

     We next control line intersections under equivariant Lipschitz maps.
Lemma 3.9 (Distortion of line intersections). Let T, T ′ be free, minimal, cocompact simplicial Fm -trees,
and let f : T → T ′ be an Fm -equivariant Lipschitz map. Put K = Lip(f ) and B = BBT(f ). Let ℓ1 , ℓ2 ⊆ T
be distinct geodesic lines, and let ℓ′1 , ℓ′2 ⊆ T ′ be the lines whose endpoint pairs are the images of those of
ℓ1 , ℓ2 under the boundary homeomorphism induced by f . If diam(ℓ1 ∩ ℓ2 ) < ∞, then
                                     diam(ℓ′1 ∩ ℓ′2 ) ≤ 2K diam(ℓ1 ∩ ℓ2 ) + 4B.

Proof. For distinct ξ, η ∈ ∂T and x ∈ T , let z be the projection of x to the geodesic line with endpoints ξ, η.
Thus
                                                  dT (x, z) = (ξ | η)x .
Choose points pn , qn on the two rays of this line based at z and tending to ξ, η, respectively. Since z ∈ [pn , qn ],
bounded backtracking gives                                              
                                          dT ′ f (z), [f (pn ), f (qn )] ≤ B.
The segments [f (pn ), f (qn )] converge on compact sets to the line with endpoints ξ ′ , η ′ . Hence that line comes
within distance B of f (z), while
                                           dT ′ (f (x), f (z)) ≤ KdT (x, z).
Since a Gromov product in a tree is the distance from the basepoint to the line joining the two boundary
points, we obtain
                                           (ξ ′ | η ′ )f (x) ≤ K(ξ | η)x + B.                                     (7)
   Put r = diam(ℓ1 ∩ ℓ2 ). If the lines meet, choose x ∈ ℓ1 ∩ ℓ2 ; otherwise choose on ℓ1 the endpoint of their
bridge. For every endpoint ξ of ℓ1 and η of ℓ2 ,
                                                     (ξ | η)x ≤ r.
Also dT ′ (f (x), ℓ′1 ) ≤ B. Since r < ∞, both pairs of lines have disjoint endpoint sets. Let J = ℓ′1 ∩ ℓ′2 and
project f (x) to x′ ∈ ℓ′1 . If |J| = p > 0, suitable endpoints ξ ′ of ℓ′1 and η ′ of ℓ′2 satisfy (ξ ′ | η ′ )x′ ≥ p/2.
Changing basepoint to f (x) and using (7) gives
                                        p/2 − B ≤ (ξ ′ | η ′ )f (x) ≤ Kr + B.
Thus p ≤ 2Kr + 4B.                                                                                                  □
                   ISOMORPHISM RIGIDITY FOR FOR GENERIC FINITELY PRESENTED GROUPS                         15


Proposition 3.10 (Uniform deterministic piece bound). Let w be an admissible tuple of nontrivial cyclically
reduced words. For every φ ∈ Out(Fm ) and every piece v of RA (φ(w)),
                                     |v| ≤ 2ΛA (φ) ρ±
                                                                
                                                    per (w) + 2m .                                      (8)
The estimate applies to self-pieces and to pieces shared by different relators.

Proof. Choose an automorphism Φ representing φ. By Lemma 3.7, a piece v of RA (φ(w)) gives distinct
translates of axes of the Φ(wi ) in TA . In the pullback realization of TA φ, these are the endpoint images,
under an optimal map TA → TA φ, of the corresponding source-axis translates. Their source intersection is
at most ρ±per (w) by Lemma 3.8. Applying Lemma 3.9 with

                                            K = ΛA (φ),        B ≤ mΛA (φ)
from (4) in Proposition 2.6 yields
        |v| ≤ OvTA (φ(w)) ≤ 2Kρ±                      ±                             ±
                                                                                                
                               per (w) + 4B ≤ 2ΛA (φ)ρper (w) + 4mΛA (φ) = 2ΛA (φ) ρper (w) + 2m .
                                                                                                          □
Remark 3.11. The estimate is deterministic; positivity in the earlier positive-word argument only replaced
signed periodic overlaps by unsigned ones.

                        4. Filling currents and abstract stability criteria

4.1. Finite-frequency stability. Recall from Definition 2.4 that
                                            KA = {T ∈ cvm : ΛA (T ) = 1},
and that KA is compact by Proposition 2.5.
  Put
                                       ∥η∥A := ⟨TA , η⟩        (η ∈ Curr(Fm ))
and
                                    SA = {η ∈ Curr(Fm ) : ∥η∥A = 1}.
Here and below, SA carries the subspace topology inherited from the weak-∗ topology on Curr(Fm ). Since
                                                 X
                                         ∥η∥A =     ⟨a, η⟩A > 0
                                                         a∈A
for every nonzero current, each projective current has a unique representative in SA .
Lemma 4.1 (Uniform convergence on the compact slice). Let µj , µ ∈ Curr(Fm ), and suppose that µj → µ.
Then:
(1)
                                    sup |⟨T, µj ⟩ − ⟨T, µ⟩| −→ 0          as j → ∞.
                                    T ∈KA
(2) The function
                                                mA (η) := min ⟨T, η⟩
                                                            T ∈KA
      is continuous on Curr(Fm ).

Proof. If (1) fails then there are ε > 0, a subsequence jk → ∞, and trees Tk ∈ KA such that
                                               |⟨Tk , µjk ⟩ − ⟨Tk , µ⟩| ≥ ε
for every k ≥ 1. After passing to a further subsequence, compactness of KA gives lim Tk = T for some
                                                                                         k→∞
T ∈ KA . Since µjk → µ, joint continuity of the intersection form gives
                                lim |⟨Tk , µjk ⟩ − ⟨Tk , µ⟩| = |⟨T, µ⟩ − ⟨T, µ⟩| = 0
                               k→∞
16                                                  I. KAPOVICH


contradicting the preceding lower bound. This proves part (1).
     For part (2), the estimate
                                   |mA (µj ) − mA (µ)| ≤ sup |⟨T, µj ⟩ − ⟨T, µ⟩|
                                                            T ∈KA

and part (1) give the continuity of mA .                                                                  □
Lemma 4.2 (Uniform filling neighborhood). Let ν ∈ SA be filling. There are a neighborhood U of ν in SA
and c > 0 such that
      (1) We have
                                               ⟨T, η⟩ ≥ cΛA (T )                                         (9)
          for every η ∈ U and every nontrivial T ∈ cvm .
      (2) For every φ ∈ Out(Fm ) we have
                                          ⟨TA φ, η⟩ = ⟨TA , φη⟩ ≥ cΛA (φ)                              (10)

Proof. Since ν is filling and KA is compact, mA (ν) > 0. Choose 0 < c < mA (ν) and a neighborhood U on
which mA (η) > c. For T ̸= 0, the tree T /ΛA (T ) lies in KA , and homogeneity gives (9), so that part (1)
holds.
     For part (2), for any φ ∈ Out(Fm ), by part (1) we have
                                  ⟨TA , φη⟩ = ⟨TA φ, η⟩ ≥ cΛA (TA φ) = cΛA (φ),
as required.                                                                                              □
Proposition 4.3 (Finite-frequency deterministic estimate). Fix q ≥ 1 and filling currents
                                                  ν1 , . . . , νq ∈ SA .
There exist an integer M ≥ 1 and constants 0 < ε < 1 and 0 < c ≤ 1 with the following property. Let
                                                W = (W1 , . . . , Wq )
be a tuple of nontrivial cyclically reduced words, and put
                                     ℓi = ∥Wi ∥A = |Wi |A ,          ℓ∗ = min ℓi .
                                                                           1≤i≤q

Suppose that, for every 1 ≤ i ≤ q and every nontrivial freely reduced word v with |v|A ≤ M ,
                                              ⟨v, Wi ⟩A

Theorem 1.3 (Finite-frequency stability criterion). Fix q ≥ 1, filling currents
                                ν1 , . . . , νq ∈ Curr(Fm )      with          ⟨TA , νi ⟩ = 1

                                     ℓi = ∥Wi ∥A = |Wi |A        (1 ≤ i ≤ q).

                                              ⟨v, Wi ⟩A
                                                        − ⟨v, νi ⟩A < ε.
                                                  ℓi
Then
                                                     ∆A (W) < λ.
In particular, W is λ-stable.

Proof. Apply Proposition 4.3 to ν1 , . . . , νq , obtaining M , ε, and 0 < c ≤ 1. Choose
                                                                  cλ

an automorphism Φ representing φ. As in the proof of Proposition 3.10, Lemma 3.7, applied to cyclically
18                                                  I. KAPOVICH


reduced representatives of the Φ(Wk ), associates to u two distinct target-axis translates whose intersection
contains a segment of length |u|. Let f : TA → TA φ be an optimal equivariant map. In the pullback
realization of TA φ, these target lines are the endpoint images under f of distinct source-axis translates
L1 , L2 ⊆ TA , where L1 belongs to component i and L2 belongs to a component j. Put
                                               d = diam(L1 ∩ L2 ).
This number is finite by Lemma 3.8.
     We claim that
                                                     d < λ′ ℓi .                                           (15)
There is nothing to prove if d = 0. If d > 0, orient the source lines compatibly along their intersection and
translate an initial vertex of the intersection to the identity. As in the proof of Lemma 3.8, the intersection
label is then a common prefix of signed periodic words arising from Wi and Wj , with distinct signed origins.
If
                                                 d ≥ min{ℓi , ℓj },
and ℓi ̸= ℓj , the full shorter cyclic word is a piece of RA (W), contradicting C ′ (λ′ ) because λ′ < 1. If
ℓi = ℓj , the two corresponding symmetrized relators agree in all ℓi positions, contradicting Lemma 3.1.
Hence d < min{ℓi , ℓj }. The corresponding members of RA (W) are distinct, and the full intersection label
is therefore a piece beginning a cyclic conjugate of Wi±1 . The C ′ (λ′ ) hypothesis gives (15).
     Apply Lemma 3.9 to the optimal map TA → TA φ. Using (4) and (15), we obtain

Taking the supremum over all pieces and all φ proves ∆A (W) < λ. The implication (6) completes the

Remark 4.4. Theorem 1.3 is a finite-data sufficient condition, although the proof does not assert that suitable
M , ε, λ′ , and n0 can be computed effectively from an arbitrary description of the filling currents νi .

4.2. Probabilistic consequences.
Definition 4.5 (Exponential concentration). Let µn be random currents taking values in SA , and let ν ∈ SA .
We say that µn concentrates exponentially at ν if, for every neighborhood U of ν in SA , there are constants
CU , cU > 0 such that
                                         P(µn ∈ / U ) ≤ CU e−cU n
for every n ≥ 1.
Remark 4.6 (Why fillingness is essential). The filling hypothesis in Proposition 4.3 and Theorem 1.3 is
essential. Let m ≥ 3, let Wn be a uniform positive word of length n in F (a2 , . . . , am ), and put
                                                    Un = a1 Wn .
Let ν0 ∈ SA be the current characterized by
                            (
                             (m − 1)−|v|A , v or v −1 is a positive word over {a2 , . . . , am },
                ⟨v, ν0 ⟩A =
                             0,             otherwise.
The normalized counting currents (n + 1)−1 ηUn concentrate exponentially at ν0 in the sense of Definition 4.5:
the Bernoulli frequencies in Wn have exponentially decaying deviation probabilities on every fixed finite
family of cylinder coordinates, while the single letter a1 affects each fixed normalized coordinate by only
O(1/n). The current ν0 is not filling. Indeed, it has zero intersection with the Bass–Serre tree of
                                           Fm = ⟨a1 ⟩ ∗ F (a2 , . . . , am ),
                     ISOMORPHISM RIGIDITY FOR FOR GENERIC FINITELY PRESENTED GROUPS                          19


because F (a2 , . . . , am ) is elliptic there.
   The denominator conclusion fails accordingly. Each Un is primitive, since a1 7→ a1 Wn , ai 7→ ai for i ≥ 2,
defines an automorphism. Hence some φn ∈ Out(Fm ) satisfies
                                                       ∥φn (Un )∥A = 1.
Because ΛA (φn ) ≥ 1, no c > 0 can satisfy
                                                  ∥φ(Un )∥A ≥ c(n + 1)ΛA (φ)
for all n and φ. Thus this nonstable family lacks precisely the filling-current denominator.

   The next two results derive the probabilistic stability estimates from the deterministic finite-frequency
estimate.
Proposition 4.7 (Filling-current denominator estimate). Fix q ≥ 1 and filling currents ν1 , . . . , νq ∈ SA .

                                 5. Uniformly random reduced words

     Put
                                       Σ = A±1 ,      d = |Σ| = 2m.

5.1. Signed periodic-overlap tails.
Lemma 5.1 (Conditional coordinates in a random cyclic word). Let n ≥ 2, and let
                                                X = X0 X1 · · · Xn−1
be uniform in Cn , and let I ⊆ Z/nZ contain no two cyclically adjacent positions. Conditional on all coordi-
nates Xj with j ∈
                / I, the variables Xi , i ∈ I, are independent. Each Xi is uniform on
                                                       −1     −1
                                                 Σ \ {Xi−1 , Xi+1 },
a set of cardinality at least d − 2 = 2m − 2.

Proof. Condition on an outside labeling of positive probability. Since I contains no adjacent positions, each
remaining reducedness constraint involves one variable and its fixed neighbors. Uniformity of admissible
completions and factorization of their number give the asserted independence and conditional laws.         □
                   ISOMORPHISM RIGIDITY FOR FOR GENERIC FINITELY PRESENTED GROUPS                                   21


Proposition 5.2 (Signed periodic-overlap tail). Fix q ≥ 1. Let Cn = (C1,n , . . . , Cq,n ) be an independent
uniformly random tuple in Cnq . There are constants C1 > 0 and 0 < θ < 1, depending only on m, q, such
that, for every n ≥ 1 and every integer R with 1 ≤ R ≤ n/4,
                                        P ρ±                   2 R
                                                        
                                           per (Cn ) ≥ R ≤ C1 n θ .                                     (18)
One may take θ = (2m − 2)−1/18 after enlarging C1 .

Proof. Fix two distinct signed origins. Equality of their length-R prefixes imposes constraints of the form
                                            Xu = Xv      or    Xu = Xv−1 .

   If the origins lie in different components, choose at least R/3 pairwise nonadjacent positions in the relevant
interval of the second component, discarding at most one endpoint at the cyclic cut. Conditional on the first
component and all other coordinates of the second, Lemma 5.1 makes these constraints independent, each
with probability at most (d − 2)−1 . Their agreement probability is therefore at most (d − 2)−R/3 , up to a
fixed factor for small R.
   Suppose the origins lie in one component. With equal signs, the constraints join s+r to t+r for 0 ≤ r < R,
so every vertex has degree at most two. Distinct r give distinct ordered edges. Repetition as an unordered
edge with reversed endpoints would imply 2(t − s) = 0 modulo n, hence t − s = n/2 and r − r′ ≡ n/2 modulo
n, impossible for 0 ≤ r, r′ < R ≤ n/4. Thus all R edges are distinct.
   If the signs are opposite, the constraint edges have the form
                                         {s + r, t − r − 1},      0 ≤ r < R.
A loop makes the event empty. Otherwise each unordered edge occurs at most twice, since an edge and one
endpoint determine r up to interchanging the endpoints. Each cyclic position occurs at most once in each
endpoint role, so the graph has at least R/2 distinct edges and maximum degree two.
   Thus the constraint graph has at least R/2 edges and maximum degree two. It has a matching of size
at least R/6; choosing one endpoint from each matching edge and then an independent set in the cyclic
adjacency graph gives a set I of size at least R/18. Orient the corresponding matching constraints toward
I. Their other endpoints are distinct and outside I, so after conditioning off I, each constraint prescribes a
different coordinate. Lemma 5.1 bounds their joint probability by
                                            (d − 2)−|I| ≤ (d − 2)−R/18 .

   There are 2qn signed origins and fewer than 4q 2 n2 ordered pairs. A union bound proves the result.               □

                                                                    q

                                 P ρ±                              2         −R/18
                                                              
                                    per (C1 , . . . , Cq ) ≥ R ≤ 4L (2m − 2)       .

Proof. The preceding proof uses only R ≤ ℓi /4 for components containing an origin, so it applies unchanged.
There are 2L signed origins and fewer than 4L2 ordered pairs.                                             □

                                        6. Positive Bernoulli words

   The abstract criterion also yields the earlier positive-word theorem without positive-specific rigidity ma-
chinery.
  For a strictly positive probability vector
                                                                         X

Lemma 6.1 (Positive Bernoulli currents are filling). Let p = (p1 , . . . , pm ) be a strictly positive probability
vector on A, and let νp be the current defined above. Then νp is filling in Curr(Fm ).

Proof. The support contains the periodic leaves of every ai and ai aj , i < j. If ⟨T, νp ⟩ = 0, the zero-
intersection criterion gives
                                        ∥ai ∥T = 0,      ∥ai aj ∥T = 0.
The fixed subtrees of the basis elements therefore intersect pairwise, and the Helly property gives a global
fixed point, contradicting minimality of a nontrivial tree.                                               □
Lemma 6.2 (Bernoulli current concentration). Let p = (p1 , . . . , pm ) be a strictly positive probability vector
on A. For every n ≥ 1, let Wn = X1 · · · Xn be a positive Bernoulli word with letter distribution p. Then
1
n ηWn concentrates exponentially at νp in the sense of Definition 4.5.

Proof. For n ≥ r, the normalized cyclic occurrence count n1 (v, Wn )A of a positive word v of length r has the
corresponding product expectation. Changing one letter affects at most r cyclic windows, so McDiarmid’s
inequality [McD89] gives exponential concentration. Negative coordinates follow by flip invariance, mixed-
sign coordinates vanish, and a finite union bound over the coordinates defining a neighborhood proves
exponential concentration in the sense of Definition 4.5. The finitely many smaller values of n are absorbed
by increasing the prefactor.                                                                                □

   We conclude this section with an almost-sure consequence for general finitely supported group random
