                               7. Generic Nielsen and Whitehead input

7.1. Whitehead’s algorithm and Whitehead automorphisms. We first briefly recall, mainly follow-
ing [KSS06, Proposition 1.2 and Definition 4.2], the form of Whitehead’s algorithm for automorphic equiva-
lence of conjugacy classes that will be used below. See also [LS77] for a detailed treatment of the topic. Put
Σ = A±1 . A Whitehead automorphism is an automorphism Θ ∈ Aut(Fm ) of one of two types. A Whitehead
automorphism of the first kind, or a relabeling automorphism, permutes Σ and commutes with inversion;
these are precisely the elements of Rel(A). A Whitehead automorphism of the second kind has a multiplier
a ∈ Σ such that, for every x ∈ Σ,
                                         Θ(x) ∈ {x, xa, a−1 x, a−1 xa};
necessarily Θ(a) = a. For fixed m ≥ 1 there are only finitely many Whitehead automorphisms, and they
generate Aut(Fm ).
   Given two cyclically reduced words u, v in Fm , Whitehead’s algorithm decides whether there exists Φ ∈
Aut(Fm ) such that Φ([u]) = [v]. For a cyclically reduced word u, call [u] minimal in its automorphic orbit
if ∥Φ(u)∥A ≥ ||u||A for every Φ ∈ Aut(Fm ). Whitehead’s length-reduction theorem says that if [u] is not
minimal, then some Whitehead automorphism Θ strictly decreases its cyclic length, ||Θ(u)||A < ||u||A . Thus
one cyclically reduces and repeatedly applies length-decreasing Whitehead automorphisms until a minimal
representative is reached. Given two conjugacy classes, one first minimizes both; unequal minimal lengths rule
out automorphic equivalence. If the minimal lengths agree, Whitehead’s peak-reduction theorem says that
the two classes are automorphically equivalent exactly when their minimal representatives can be joined by a
finite sequence of Whitehead automorphisms along which cyclic length remains constant. Since there are only
finitely many cyclic words of a fixed length, this procedure requires only a finite search. In the terminology
of [KSS06], minimization is the “easy part” of Whitehead’s algorithm (which runs in O(|u|2A ) time), while
28                                                I. KAPOVICH


the length-preserving search is the “hard part” requiring a priori exponential time in max{|u|A , |v|A }). The
search form records the Whitehead moves and hence produces an explicit automorphism when the classes
are equivalent. Strict minimality, recalled below, makes this second stage especially simple.

7.2. Nielsen uniqueness and polynomial recognition. We first record a small algorithmic refinement
of the readability conditions used in the Arzhantseva–Ol’shanskii method. The original complexity estimate
in [KS05] is exponential. The point below is that, when the rank bound is fixed, a witness graph has
uniformly bounded topological complexity, so the labels of its maximal arcs may be chosen among subwords
of the input word. This is analogous to the subword enumeration used for the quartic recognition algorithm
in [KS09, Lemma 3.10]; we will only need a polynomial bound here.
   Here an A-labelled graph is an oriented graph whose oriented edges have labels in A±1 , with the reverse
orientation carrying the inverse label. Edge counts below refer to unoriented edges, and the label of a path
is obtained by reading its oriented edge labels in order.
Lemma 7.1 (Polynomial recognition of fixed-rank readability). Fix m ≥ 2, an integer R ≥ 1, and a rational
number 0 < µ ≤ 1. Let w be a nontrivial freely reduced word over A±1 , of length ℓ. Each of the following
conditions is decidable in deterministic time polynomial in ℓ:
(1) there exists a finite connected A-labelled graph Γ with at most µℓ unoriented edges and rank π1 (Γ) ≤ R
    in which w labels a reduced path;
(2) there exists such a graph Γ which, in addition, has a vertex of degree strictly less than 2m.
(3) For fixed parameters, the µ-readability and (µ, L)-readability conditions of [KS05, Definitions 4.1–4.2]
    are polynomial-time decidable.

Proof. Suppose first that a graph Γ as in part (1) exists, and let p be a reduced path labelled by w. Replace
Γ by the connected subgraph H consisting of the edges traversed by p. This does not increase the number
of edges or the rank, and every edge of H is traversed by p.
   Every degree-one vertex of H is an endpoint of p: otherwise p would have to enter that vertex and
immediately traverse the same edge backwards. Thus H has at most two degree-one vertices. If r =
rank π1 (H) ≤ R, the identity          X
                                           (deg(x) − 2) = 2r − 2
                                        x∈V (H)
shows that the number of vertices of degree at least three is at most 2R. Mark the initial and terminal
vertices of p and suppress every other degree-two vertex. The resulting topological graph therefore has a
number of vertices and edges bounded by a constant depending only on R; for example, it has at most 2R + 2
marked or branching vertices and at most 3R + 1 topological edges.
   Choose an orientation on each topological edge. Once the reduced path p enters the interior of a maximal
arc (a path whose internal vertices have degree two), it must continue along that arc until it reaches an
endpoint of the arc; the initial and terminal vertices of p have already been marked. Since every edge of
H is traversed by p, the label of every oriented topological edge is therefore a nonempty subword of w or
w−1 . There are O(ℓ2 ) possible such labels. Since there are only finitely many topological graph types with
marked initial and terminal vertices, and only a bounded number of topological edges depending on R alone,
all possible labelled graphs H can therefore be enumerated in polynomial time.
   For each candidate, expand the topological edges and check the edge and rank bounds. A finite-state
dynamic program, propagating the possible current vertices while the letters of w are read, decides in
polynomial time whether w labels a path in the candidate. Because w is freely reduced, any path with
label w is automatically reduced. The expanded candidate has O(ℓ) edges, so each candidate is checked in
polynomial time. This proves part (1).
   For part (2), again let H be the union of the edges traversed by p. If H already has a vertex of degree
less than 2m, the preceding enumeration applies unchanged. Otherwise the required low-degree vertex of Γ
                  ISOMORPHISM RIGIDITY FOR FOR GENERIC FINITELY PRESENTED GROUPS                              29


lies outside H, so H is a proper subgraph of the connected graph Γ. Hence at least one edge of Γ \ H is
incident to H, and therefore
                                          |E(H)| + 1 ≤ |E(Γ)| ≤ µℓ.
Attach one pendant edge, with any label, to an arbitrary vertex of H. The resulting connected labelled
graph has the same rank as H, has at most µℓ edges, still contains the path labelled w, and has a degree-one
vertex. Thus it suffices, for each candidate H from part (1), to check either that H already has a vertex of
degree less than 2m or that the edge bound allows one additional pendant edge. This is again polynomial.
   The definitions of µ-readability and (µ, L)-readability in [KS05] are precisely the two cases above with
fixed rank bounds m − 1 and L, respectively. In the latter definition the path is not explicitly required to
be reduced, but this is automatic when its label is the freely reduced word w.                            □
Theorem 7.2 (Kapovich–Schupp, with polynomial recognition). Fix m ≥ 2 and q ≥ 1. There are subsets
                                           Pm,q (n) ⊆ Cnq           (n ≥ 1)
and constants C, c > 0 such that:
(1) For every n ≥ 1,
                                            |Pm,q (n)|
                                                        ≥ 1 − Ce−cn .
                                                |Cn |q
(2) For every n ≥ 1, membership in Pm,q (n) is decidable in deterministic polynomial time in n.
(3) For every n ≥ 1 and every R = (r1 , . . . , rq ) ∈ Pm,q (n), put
                                        GR = ⟨a1 , . . . , am | r1 , . . . , rq ⟩.
    Then GR is torsion-free, one-ended, and non-elementary hyperbolic, every subgroup generated by at
    most m − 1 elements is free, and every m-tuple generating a nonfree subgroup is Nielsen-equivalent to
    the standard tuple (a1 , . . . , am ), where ai denotes the image of ai in GR .
(4) For every n ≥ 1 and every R ∈ Pm,q (n), with GR as in part (3), every nonfree subgroup of GR generated
    by at most m elements is all of GR , every automorphism of GR lifts to an automorphism of Fm , and
    GR is co-Hopfian.

Proof. Choose fixed rational parameters λ, µ and an integer L as in the proof of [KS05, Theorem B], and take
the corresponding Kapovich–Schupp class. The group-theoretic conclusions are those of [KS05, Theorem B].
Their theorem is stated in the cumulative few-relator model. If
                                                     X
                                              Bncr =      |Cℓ |,
                                                          1≤ℓ≤n

then (1) gives Bncr ≍ |Cn | ≍ (2m − 1)n . The bad equal-length tuples lie in the bad cumulative set, while the
cumulative ambient set has size (Bncr )q ≍ |Cn |q ; hence exponential genericity transfers to the equal-length
sphere.
   It remains only to improve the recognition bound stated in [KS05]. By [KS05, Definition 4.3], membership
in the relevant class requires the C ′ (λ) condition, absence of proper-power relators, and the requirement that
every subword of a cyclic conjugate of a relator having length at least half that relator length be neither µ-
readable nor (µ, L)-readable. Small cancellation and proper-power detection are polynomial-time decidable.
There are only polynomially many relevant cyclic subwords, and Lemma 7.1 tests each readability condition
in polynomial time, with degree depending only on the fixed parameters. Thus membership in Pm,q (n)
is polynomial-time decidable. This is the same finite-subword principle that yields the explicit quartic
recognition bound in the modular-group setting of [KS09, Theorem A and Lemma 3.10]; no particular
polynomial degree is needed here.
   Part (4) follows as in [KS05]: Nielsen moves preserve generated subgroups, automorphisms send the
standard tuple to generating tuples, and an injective endomorphism has nonfree image generated by at most
m elements.                                                                                            □
30                                                    I. KAPOVICH


7.3. Generic Whitehead input. A cyclically reduced word w is strictly minimal if every non-inner White-
head automorphism of the second kind strictly increases its cyclic length. Let Zm be the class denoted Z
in [KSS06, Definition 8.6]. Thus its elements are strictly minimal and root-free, no nontrivial relabeling
sends one to a conjugate of itself, and no relabeling sends one to a conjugate of its inverse. The following
result is due to Kapovich–Schupp–Shpilrain [KSS06]:
Theorem 7.3 (Kapovich–Schupp–Shpilrain). Fix m ≥ 2. Then the following hold.
(1) The subsets Zm ∩ Cn are exponentially generic in Cn as n → ∞, and membership in Zm is decidable in
    linear time.
(2) If w ∈ Zm , then
                                            StabOut(Fm ) ([w]) = {1}.
(3) If u is strictly minimal and v is cyclically reduced with |u| = |v|, then [u] and [v] lie in the same
    Out(Fm )-orbit if and only if a relabeling automorphism sends u to a cyclic shift of v.
(4) On any pair of cyclically reduced input words for which at least one input lies in the automorphic orbit
    of a strictly minimal word, Whitehead’s algorithm, in search form, runs in at most quadratic time in the
    total input length. If both inputs are strictly minimal, orbit testing is linear.

Proof. Theorem B, Theorem 8.5, and Proposition 8.7 of [KSS06] give genericity and the stabilizer statement.
Sphere and cumulative exponential genericity are equivalent because |Cn | ≍ (2m − 1)n and the cumulative
ball has comparable size. Linear membership tests strict minimality and finitely many relabeling and inverse-
conjugacy conditions. Theorem A(3)–(5) gives the orbit and complexity claims; recording the Whitehead
moves yields the search form.                                                                              □

                                 8. Greendlinger normal-closure rigidity

     For a tuple R = (r1 , . . . , rq ) of elements of a free group F = F (X), denote
                                               NR = ⟨⟨r1 , . . . , rq ⟩⟩ ⊴ F,
the normal closure of R in F . Similarly, for a set R ⊆ F , write NR = ⟨⟨R⟩⟩ ⊴ F .
   We use a modern formulation, Theorem 8.2 of Greendlinger’s classic analogue [Gre61] of Magnus’s theo-
rem. The original statement uses terminology predating standard small-cancellation language. The formu-
lation below follows from Greendlinger’s argument; see also Proposition 6.5 of [KS09] for a similar statement
for small-cancellation quotients of the modular group.
   For completeness, we give a self-contained proof of Theorem 8.2 using modern small cancellation theory
tools. We use the notation and terminology of Chapter V of [LS77]. There a planar map M is called a
(3, 6)-map if every vertex v has degree d(v) ≥ 3 and every interior region D has degree d(D) ≥ 6. For a
boundary region D, the quantity i(D) denotes its interior degree, that is, the number of interior edges in
the boundary cycle ∂D. We use the standard combinatorial-disc convention that each region is a closed
2-cell equipped with its boundary cycle; intersections and consecutive arcs below are understood on these
boundary cycles. To a van Kampen diagram ∆ over a symmetrized presentation ⟨X | R⟩, one associates a
connected and simply connected planar map M by suppressing degree-two vertices. Whereas the oriented
edges of ∆ are labelled by elements of X ±1 , the edges of M are labelled by nontrivial freely reduced words
in F (X).
   Lemma 2.2 of Chapter V of [LS77] implies that the planar map associated to a reduced van Kampen
diagram over a C ′ (1/6) presentation is a (3, 6)-map.
   The following consequence is likely standard, but we include a proof because we have not found this
precise formulation in the literature.
                  ISOMORPHISM RIGIDITY FOR FOR GENERIC FINITELY PRESENTED GROUPS                          31


Lemma 8.1 (Region length versus boundary length). Let ∆ be a reduced van Kampen diagram over a
C ′ (1/6) presentation ⟨X | R⟩. Suppose that ∆ contains at least two regions and has no vertices of degree
one. Let
                                           w = w(∆) ∈ (X ∪ X −1 )∗
be the word, not necessarily freely reduced, labelling the boundary cycle ∂∆.
  Then, for every region D of ∆, if µ(D) is the label of ∂D, then
                                              |µ(D)| < |w(∆)|.

Proof. We induct on the number t of regions of ∆.
  Suppose first that t = 2, and denote the two regions by D and D′ . If D and D′ have no common boundary
edge, then the boundary walk of ∆ traverses the entire boundary cycles of both regions and may also traverse
one-dimensional connecting portions. Hence
                                         |w(∆)| ≥ |µ(D)| + |µ(D′ )|.
Thus the required strict inequality holds for both regions.
   Suppose that D and D′ have a common boundary edge. Since ∆ is simply connected, their common
boundary edges form a single arc: two disjoint common arcs would create a nontrivial loop in the union of
the two closed regions. Let v be its label. Since ∆ is reduced, v is a piece. Therefore
                                         |µ(D)|                    |µ(D′ )|
                                   |v| <            and      |v| <          .
                                            6                         6
Moreover,
                                       |w(∆)| = |µ(D)| + |µ(D′ )| − 2|v|.
It follows that
                                    |w(∆)| − |µ(D)| = |µ(D′ )| − 2|v| > 0,
and, symmetrically,
                                    |w(∆)| − |µ(D′ )| = |µ(D)| − 2|v| > 0.
This proves the result when t = 2.
   Now let t > 2 and assume that the conclusion holds for every reduced van Kampen diagram satisfying
the hypotheses of the lemma and having t′ regions, where 2 ≤ t′ < t.
   If ∆ is not a disc diagram, cut the planar complex at its cut vertices and consider the maximal disc
subdiagrams containing regions. Distinct such disc components meet, if at all, only at cut vertices, and
the boundary walk of ∆ is obtained by concatenating their boundary walks together with possible one-
dimensional connecting portions, which are traversed twice. Since there is more than one disc component,
every component containing a region has fewer than t regions, and
                                                   X
                                          |w(∆)| ≥     |w(∆′ )|.
                                                         ∆′
Let D be a region contained in a disc component ∆ . If ∆′ has one region, then
                                                     ′

                                         |µ(D)| ≤ |w(∆′ )| < |w(∆)|.
If ∆′ has at least two regions, the inductive hypothesis gives
                                         |µ(D)| < |w(∆′ )| ≤ |w(∆)|.
Thus the result follows, and we may assume that ∆ is a disc diagram.
   Let M be the planar map associated to ∆. Since M is a (3, 6)-map, Theorem 4.3 of Chapter V of [LS77]
gives
                                          X ∗
                                              [4 − i(D)] ≥ 6,
                                              M
32                                               I. KAPOVICH


where the sum is taken over the boundary regions D for which ∂D ∩ ∂M is a consecutive part of ∂M . Since
t > 1, every such region has i(D) ≥ 1, and hence every positive summand is at most 3. Hence at least two
distinct boundary regions D1 , D2 occur in this sum with
                                      1 ≤ i(D1 ) ≤ 3,     1 ≤ i(D2 ) ≤ 3.

   We first remove only the region D1 from ∆. Let p1 be the total length, in the original X ±1 -labelling, of
the interior part of ∂D1 , and let e1 be the length of the exterior part ∂D1 ∩ ∂∆. Every edge of the associated
map contained in the interior part of ∂D1 is labelled by a piece. Hence
                                                      |µ(D1 )|   |µ(D1 )|
                                          p1 < i(D1 )          ≤          .
                                                         6          2
Since e1 = |µ(D1 )| − p1 , we have e1 > p1 .
   Because ∂D1 ∩ ∂M is a consecutive part of the boundary cycle of M , its complementary interior part on
the boundary cycle of D1 is also a single consecutive arc. Thus D1 is a boundary ear: it is attached to the
closure of the remaining disc diagram precisely along this interior arc. Deleting the open 2-cell D1 together
with the open exterior boundary arc therefore leaves a connected and simply connected subdiagram with
t − 1 regions. We denote this subdiagram by ∆1 . On the boundary walk, this operation replaces the exterior
arc of length e1 by the interior attaching arc of length p1 . Thus its boundary length is
                                          |w(∆)| − e1 + p1 < |w(∆)|.
By construction, ∆1 is a disc van Kampen diagram with no degree-one vertices (although the label of the
boundary cycle of ∆1 is not necessarily cyclically reduced even if the label of the boundary cycle of ∆ is
cyclically reduced.). Since ∆ was a reduced diagram, ∆1 is also reduced. The digram ∆1 has exactly t−1 ≥ 2
regions, contains every region of ∆ other than D1 , and satisfies
                                              |w(∆1 )| < |w(∆)|.
Thus the inductive hypothesis applied to ∆1 and gives, for every region D ̸= D1 of ∆,
                                          |µ(D)| < |w(∆1 )| < |w(∆)|.
In particular, this estimate holds for D2 .
   A symmetric argument with removing D2 from ∆ yields |µ(D1 )| < |w(∆)|, completing the inductive
step.                                                                                           □

  The argument permits intermediate boundary labels that are not freely reduced, even when the original
boundary label is freely and cyclically reduced.
Theorem 8.2 (Greendlinger-type normal-closure rigidity). Let R and S be symmetrized sets of nontrivial
cyclically reduced words in a free group F = F (X), and suppose that both R and S satisfy C ′ (1/6). If
                                                  NR = NS ,
then
                                                   R = S.

Proof. Suppose R ̸= S, and choose a shortest element z of the symmetric difference R △ S. After inter-
changing the two sets, assume that z ∈ R \ S. Since z ∈ NS , there is a reduced van Kampen disc diagram ∆
over ⟨X | S⟩ whose boundary label is z. The word z is cyclically reduced, so ∆ has no boundary spurs and
hence no vertices of degree one. Moreover, ∆ has at least two regions: a one-region diagram would imply
that z ∈ S, since S is symmetrized.
   By Lemma 8.1, every region label s ∈ S occurring in ∆ satisfies |s| < |z|. The minimal choice of z
therefore implies that every such s belongs to R ∩ S.
                  ISOMORPHISM RIGIDITY FOR FOR GENERIC FINITELY PRESENTED GROUPS                               33


   Greendlinger’s lemma [LS77, Chapter V, Theorem 4.4] gives a boundary region of ∆ whose boundary
shares with ∂∆ a segment labelled by a word v satisfying
                                                         |s|
                                                   |v| >     ,
                                                          2
where s ∈ R ∩ S is the label of that region. After taking suitable cyclic conjugates, and inverses if necessary,
two elements of R, one of length |s| and the other of length |z|, have v as a common initial segment. These
elements are distinct because |s| < |z|. Thus v is a piece for R, contradicting
                                                               |s|   |s|
                                                    |v| >          >
                                                                2     6
and the C ′ (1/6) condition for R.                                                                             □

  The sets X, R, and S in Theorem 8.2 need not be finite.
Corollary 8.3 (Irredundant tuple form). Let q, t ≥ 1 and 0 < λ ≤ 1/6. Let
                                     R = (r1 , . . . , rq ),       S = (s1 , . . . , st )
be irredundant tuples of nontrivial elements of Fm . Suppose that the symmetrizations of cyclically reduced
forms of both tuples satisfy C ′ (λ). If
                                                 NR = NS ,
then q = t, and after a permutation of the indices every ri is conjugate in Fm to some s±1
                                                                                        j .

Proof. Choose cyclically reduced conjugates ui of the ri and vj of the sj , and let R and S be their sym-
metrizations. Since λ ≤ 1/6, both sets satisfy C ′ (1/6), and
                                              NR = NR = NS = NS .
Theorem 8.2 gives R = S. The cyclic-permutation-and-inversion orbits in a symmetrized set are its sym-
metrized relator classes. Irredundancy says that the entries of R and S represent, respectively, q and t
distinct such classes. Hence q = t, and the asserted correspondence follows.                          □
Remark 8.4. Root-freeness is not needed in Theorem 8.2 or Corollary 8.3. Irredundancy is needed only to
recover the number of entries in a tuple: repetitions or duplicate conjugacy classes do not change a normal
closure. Greendlinger’s shortest-unmatched-relator argument removes any common-length requirement.

                                        10. The generic rigidity class

     For a cyclic word w, write sht (w) for cyclic shift by t positions.
     Fix m ≥ 2 and q ≥ 1. For n ≥ 3, let Γm,q,n be the group of transformations of Cnq generated by:
  (i) one global relabeling Θ ∈ Rel(A);
 (ii) a permutation of the q components;
(iii) independent inversion of the components;
(iv) independent cyclic shifts of the components.
Thus every element has the form
                                                                                 q
                                       (r1 , . . . , rq ) 7−→ shti Θ(rσ(i) )εi     i=1
                                                                                         ,                  (25)
where σ ∈ Sym(q), εi ∈ {±1}, and ti ∈ Z/nZ.
Lemma 10.1 (The obvious symmetry group). Fix m ≥ 2, q ≥ 1, and an integer n ≥ 3. Then the action of
Γm,q,n on Cnq defined in (25) is faithful and
                                               |Γm,q,n | = 2m+q m! q! nq .                                  (26)
                  ISOMORPHISM RIGIDITY FOR FOR GENERIC FINITELY PRESENTED GROUPS                               35


Proof. The rotations and inversions of the individual cyclic words form a product of q dihedral groups of
order 2n; component permutations permute these factors, while the global relabeling group has order 2m m!
and commutes with rotations and component permutations.
   To see faithfulness, suppose that a transformation acts identically on all tuples. Varying the components
independently first forces the component permutation to be trivial. On each component the resulting map
has the form
                                                w 7−→ sht Θ(w)ε .
                                                                 

Applying it to the constant cyclic words an , for all a ∈ A±1 , shows, on each component, that either ε = 1
and Θ = 1, or ε = −1 and Θ is the global inversion relabeling. Since Θ is global, the same alternative
holds on every component. In the first case a positive cyclic word with no nontrivial rotational period forces
every ti = 0. In the second case the map on the i-th component is a prescribed reflection of the n cyclic
positions. Since n ≥ 3, choose two positions interchanged by that reflection, put different positive basis
letters at those positions, and fill all remaining positions with one of them. The resulting word is aperiodic
and is not fixed by the prescribed reflection. Hence the second case is impossible. Thus the action is faithful,
and the semidirect-product description gives (26).                                                            □

  Let Pm,q (n) be the Kapovich–Schupp class from Theorem 7.2. Replace it by its Γm,q,n -invariant core

recognizable.

and q. Accordingly, when we call the classes Qm,q (n) finitely specified, we mean that for fixed m, q this finite
rational auxiliary data has been chosen once and for all.

Lemma 10.3 (Deterministic consequences). Fix n ≥ 1 and let R ∈ Qm,q (n). Let NR ⊴ Fm be the normal

(1) R is admissible and λ0 -stable;

Proposition 10.4 (Genericity and effectiveness). Fix m ≥ 2 and q ≥ 1, and let Qm,q (n) be the classes from
Definition 10.2. Then the following hold.
(1) There are constants C, c1 > 0 such that, for every n ≥ 1,
                                           |Qm,q (n)|
                                                      ≥ 1 − Ce−c1 n .
                                             |Cn |q
(2) For every n ≥ 1, membership in Qm,q (n) is decidable in deterministic polynomial time in n.

Proof. Condition (Q1) is exponentially generic by Theorem 7.2 and the polynomial-size invariant-core con-
struction. Lemma 5.6 and a finite union bound treat (Q2). Failure of (Q3) implies
                                                      cλ0
                                           ρ±
                                            per (R) ≥     n − 2m,
                                                       2
so Proposition 5.2 treats (Q3). The class Zm is exponentially generic by Theorem 7.3.
   It remains to treat tuple symmetries. If every component lies in Zm , no nonidentity element of Γm,q,n
with trivial component permutation can fix the tuple: the defining properties of Zm exclude nontrivial
relabeling and inverse-conjugacy, while root-freeness excludes nonzero cyclic rotations. If the component
permutation is nontrivial, a fixed tuple satisfies, for some i ̸= j, an equality between ri and a relabeling,
inversion, and cyclic shift of rj . Since these operations preserve the uniform measure on Cn , the probability
of any prescribed such equality is |Cn |−1 . A union bound over the polynomially many elements of Γm,q,n
gives an exponentially small probability.
   For effectiveness, Theorem 7.2(2) and the polynomial-size invariant-core construction show that (Q1) is
polynomial-time decidable for fixed m, q. The finite cylinder inequalities in (Q2), signed periodic overlaps
in (Q3), membership in Zm , and all finite symmetry checks are polynomial-time decidable as well. Thus the
total membership test is polynomial-time.                                                                 □
Lemma 10.5 (Essential cyclic splittings). Let G be a torsion-free hyperbolic group. Suppose that G admits
a nontrivial graph-of-groups splitting over infinite cyclic edge groups such that every edge group has infinite
index in each incident vertex group. Then Out(G) contains an element of infinite order.

Proof. Collapse all but one edge orbit in the Bass–Serre tree. The resulting one-edge splitting retains the
infinite-index condition and is either an amalgam
                                                G = G1 ∗C G2
                   ISOMORPHISM RIGIDITY FOR FOR GENERIC FINITELY PRESENTED GROUPS                                    37


or an HNN extension
                                        G = ⟨H, t | t−1 C− t = C+ ⟩,
where the displayed edge groups are infinite cyclic. In particular, G1 , G2 , and H are noncyclic.
    In the amalgam case, choose 1 ̸= c ∈ C and let δ fix G1 pointwise and act on G2 by conjugation by c.
This is the standard Dehn twist. If δ k were inner for some k ̸= 0, say δ k = ad(h), then h would centralize
G1 . Hence h = 1: if h ̸= 1, then the cyclic centralizer CG (h) would contain the noncyclic group G1 . Thus
δ k would be the identity. But G2 is noncyclic, whereas CG (ck ) is cyclic, so some g ∈ G2 does not commute
with ck and
                                             δ k (g) = ck gc−k ̸= g,
a contradiction.
   In the HNN case, choose 1 ̸= c ∈ C− and define δ by δ|H = id and δ(t) = ct. Since C− is cyclic, this
preserves the defining relation. If a nonzero power δ k were inner, its conjugating element would centralize
the noncyclic group H and hence would be trivial. This would make δ k the identity, contrary to
                                                    δ k (t) = ck t ̸= t.
Thus the outer class of δ has infinite order. This is the standard Dehn-twist argument; compare [GL15,
Theorem 1.2].                                                                                       □

10.1. Proof of generic few-relator rigidity.
Theorem B (Generic few-relator rigidity). Fix m ≥ 2 and q ≥ 1. For a finite tuple R = (r1 , . . . , rs ) of
elements of Fm , write
                                     GR = ⟨a1 , . . . , am | r1 , . . . , rs ⟩,
and denote by ai the image of ai in GR . There are finitely specified subsets
                                             Qm,q (n) ⊆ Cnq          (n ≥ 1)
and constants C, c > 0 such that:
(1) For every n ≥ 1, a uniform random tuple in Cnq belongs to Qm,q (n) with probability at least 1 − Ce−cn .
    Membership in Qm,q (n) is decidable in deterministic polynomial time in n.
(2) Every q-tuple R ∈ Qm,q (n) is irredundant, root-free, and 1/6-stable.
(3) If R = (r1 , . . . , rq ) ∈ Qm,q (n), then GR is torsion-free, one-ended, and non-elementary hyperbolic; every
    subgroup generated by at most m − 1 elements is free; every m-tuple generating a nonfree subgroup is
    Nielsen-equivalent to the standard tuple (a1 , . . . , am ); and GR is co-Hopfian, meaning that every injective
    endomorphism of GR is surjective.
(4) If R = (r1 , . . . , rq ) ∈ Qm,q (n), then GR is complete, meaning that its center is trivial and every auto-
    morphism of GR is inner. Its boundary is one-dimensional, connected, and has no local cut points, and
    hence is homeomorphic to the Menger curve or the Sierpiński carpet. If q ≥ m − 1, then ∂GR is the
    Menger curve.
(5) Let R = (r1 , . . . , rq ) ∈ Qm,q (n), and let S = (s1 , . . . , st ) be an irredundant tuple of nontrivial elements
    of Fm whose symmetrization of cyclically reduced representatives satisfies C ′ (1/6). Then GR ∼             = GS if
    and only if t = q and there are Φ ∈ Aut(Fm ), σ ∈ Sym(q), signs εi ∈ {±1}, and gi ∈ Fm such that
                                        Φ(ri ) = gi sεσ(i)
                                                       i
                                                           gi−1      (1 ≤ i ≤ q).
(6) If R = (r1 , . . . , rq ) ∈ Qm,q (n) and S = (s1 , . . . , sq ) ∈ Qm,q (n′ ), then GR ∼
                                                                                          = GS if and only if n = n′ and
    there are Θ ∈ Rel(A), σ ∈ Sym(q), and signs εi ∈ {±1} such that, for each i = 1, . . . , q, the word si is
    a cyclic permutation of Θ(rσ(i) )εi .

Proof. Proposition 10.4 gives part (1). Lemma 10.3(1) gives part (2): admissibility means root-freeness and
irredundancy, and λ0 -stability with λ0 = 1/12 implies 1/6-stability. Lemma 10.3 together with Theorem 7.2
gives part (3).
38                                                  I. KAPOVICH


  We prove completeness. Let R = (r1 , . . . , rq ) ∈ Qm,q (n) and let Ψ ∈ Aut(GR ). By Nielsen uniqueness,
Ψ lifts to Φ ∈ Aut(Fm ) with Φ(NR ) = NR . Stability and Corollary 8.3 give a permutation σ, signs εi , and
conjugators gi such that
                                                          εi
                                             Φ(ri ) = gi rσ(i) gi−1 .                                   (29)
                     ε1
The words r1 and rσ(1)   are strictly minimal and have the same length. Theorem 7.3(3) gives a relabeling
                                              ε1
Θ ∈ Rel(A) carrying r1 to a cyclic shift of rσ(1) . Hence Θ−1 Φ fixes [r1 ], and the trivial outer stabilizer of r1
gives
                                             [Φ] = [Θ] ∈ Out(Fm ).
Using this in (29) shows that the global relabeling Θ, the component permutation σ, the signs εi , and
suitable cyclic shifts define an element of Γm,q,n fixing R. Condition (Q4) makes that element trivial.
Therefore [Φ] = 1, so every automorphism of GR is inner. The center of a non-elementary torsion-free
hyperbolic group is trivial, and hence GR is complete.
   Because R is root-free and satisfies C ′ (λ0 ) with λ0 < 1/6, the classical asphericity theorem for C(6) pre-
sentations without proper-power relators [LS77, Chapter V, Theorem 13.3] makes the presentation complex
a finite two-dimensional K(GR , 1), with
                                               χ(GR ) = 1 − m + q.                                              (30)
Since GR is one-ended and nonfree, Stallings–Swan gives cd(GR ) = 2, and Bestvina–Mess [BM91] gives
dim ∂GR = 1.
   By Lemma 10.5 and completeness, GR admits no essential splitting over an infinite cyclic subgroup, where
“essential” means that every edge group has infinite index in each incident vertex group.
   Since GR is one-ended, it has no splitting over a finite subgroup. As it is torsion-free, its two-ended
subgroups are infinite cyclic, so it admits no essential splitting over a two-ended subgroup. Moreover, GR is
not virtually cocompact Fuchsian, since in the torsion-free case this would make it a closed surface group,
whose outer automorphism group is infinite. The boundary of a one-ended hyperbolic group is connected and
locally connected. Bowditch’s construction underlying [Bow98, Theorem 6.2] shows that a local cut point
would yield a nontrivial splitting over a two-ended subgroup. In the standard reduction of the canonical graph
of groups, each cyclic vertex of this type has valence at least two; collapsing one incident edge absorbs that
vertex into a non-two-ended vertex group while leaving another edge, and the resulting splitting is nontrivial
and essential in the above sense. Hence ∂GR has no local cut points. Since dim ∂GR = 1, Kapovich–
Kleiner [KK00, Theorem 1] gives the circle/Menger-curve/Sierpiński-carpet alternatives. The circle case
is excluded by the preceding non-Fuchsian observation, leaving the Menger curve or the Sierpiński carpet.
If q ≥ m − 1, then (30) gives χ(GR ) ≥ 0, whereas a torsion-free hyperbolic group with Sierpiński-carpet
boundary has negative Euler characteristic by [KK00, Corollary 8]. This proves part (4).
   For part (5), Lemma 10.3 makes R irredundant and 1/6-stable, since λ0 < 1/6, and supplies Nielsen
uniqueness. Proposition 9.2, with parameter 1/6, gives the assertion.
   For part (6), let R ∈ Qm,q (n) and S = (s1 , . . . , sq ) ∈ Qm,q (n′ ), and suppose GR ∼
                                                                                          = GS . Part (5) gives Φ, σ,
signs, and conjugators. Strict minimality of the components gives n′ ≥ n by applying Φ to a component of R,
and n ≥ n′ by applying Φ−1 to the corresponding component of S; hence n = n′ . Applying Theorem 7.3(3)
to one matched pair gives a relabeling Θ with the same outer class as Φ, because the source component has
trivial outer stabilizer. The full family of relations therefore has the form
                                               si = shti Θ(rσ(i) )εi .
                                                                       

The converse is immediate.                                                                                         □

                              11. Isomorphism algorithms and enumeration

11.1. Isomorphism algorithms. Fix R = (r1 , . . . , rq ) ∈ Qm,q (n0 ). The parameters m, q, n0 , the tuple R,
and the neighborhood data defining Qm,q are constants. For a comparison tuple S = (s1 , . . . , st ) put
                                                         t
                                                         X
                                                   N=          |sj |A .
                                                         j=1

Lemma 11.1 (Checking the comparison promise). Fix q ≥ 1. Let S = (s1 , . . . , st ) be a finite tuple of
words over A±1 , and let N be their total input length. In O(N 2 ) time one can determine whether all of the
following hold:
(1) t = q, and every sj is nontrivial and cyclically reduced;
(2) the tuple S is irredundant;
(3) the symmetrization of S satisfies C ′ (1/6).

Proof. A linear scan checks part (1). Part (2) is checked by testing each pair for cyclic conjugacy up to
inversion, using a doubled word. Since q is fixed after part (1) has passed, the total time is O(N 2 ).
   For part (3), form the doubled blocks sj sj and s−1       −1
                                                         j sj , separated by distinct fixed markers outside A
                                                                                                             ±1
                                                                                                                .
A generalized suffix array and longest-common-prefix data can be built in O(N log N ) time. For each cyclic
relator use only starting positions in the first copy of its doubled block, and cap every longest-common-
prefix value at the length of that relator, so that no comparison runs beyond one cyclic turn. Group starts
representing the same member of the symmetrized set and discard repetitions. There are O(N ) remaining
starts; checking every pair for a common prefix whose length is at least one sixth of the shorter relator costs
O(N 2 ) in total. The separating markers prevent comparisons from crossing between blocks. This condition
is exactly the failure of the strict C ′ (1/6) inequality, so its absence is exactly C ′ (1/6).               □
Lemma 11.2 (Search output from a fixed strictly minimal word). Let N ≥ 1, let u be a fixed strictly
minimal cyclically reduced word, and suppose that a cyclically reduced word v of length at most N lies in the
same Out(Fm )-orbit as u. The search form of Whitehead’s algorithm produces
                                          Φ = Θk · · · Θ1 ,        k = O(N ),
where the Θi are Whitehead automorphisms, Φ[u] = [v], and every prefix image Θj · · · Θ1 [u] has cyclic length
O(N ). The search takes O(N 2 ) time.

Proof. By Theorem 7.3(4), Whitehead’s algorithm takes O(N 2 ) time and records its moves. Minimize v by
length-decreasing Whitehead moves. There are at most N such moves and all intermediate cyclic lengths are
at most N . Since u is strictly minimal and equivalent to v, the terminal minimum is obtained from u by a
relabeling and a cyclic shift, by Theorem 7.3(3). Start with this fixed-length move and reverse the recorded
minimization path. This process gives the stated Whitehead word and prefix-length bound.                   □
Lemma 11.3 (Applying a recorded search to a fixed tuple). Let N ≥ 1 and let u ∈ Fm \ {1} be fixed.
Suppose that, for some c > 0,
                                       
                                    ηu
                                T,        ≥ cΛA (T ) (T ∈ cvm \ {0}).                         (31)
                                   ∥u∥A
Let R = (r1 , . . . , rq ) be a fixed tuple of nontrivial elements of Fm . Suppose
                                          Φ = Θk · · · Θ1 ,        k = O(N ),
where the Θi are Whitehead generators. Put
                             Φj = Θj · · · Θ1 ∈ Aut(Fm ),           φj = [Φj ] ∈ Out(Fm ),
and suppose that every prefix image Φj [u] has cyclic length O(N ). Then cyclically reduced representatives of
all Φ[ri ] can be computed in O(N 2 ) time.
40                                                 I. KAPOVICH


Proof. Taking T = TA φj in (31) gives
                                           ∥Φj (u)∥A ≥ c∥u∥A ΛA (φj ),
so ΛA (φj ) = O(N ). An equivariant ΛA (φj )-Lipschitz map TA → TA φj bounds translation lengths, and
hence
                                     ∥Φj (ri )∥A ≤ ΛA (φj )∥ri ∥A = O(N )
for every fixed component. Apply the Whitehead generators successively to cyclically reduced representatives
and cyclically reduce after each step. Since m is fixed, each Whitehead generator replaces every basis letter
by a word of uniformly bounded length, and substitution followed by free and cyclic reduction is linear in
the current word length. Thus each stage costs O(N ); there are O(N ) stages, and q is fixed.              □

Theorem C (Isomorphism algorithms). Fix m ≥ 2 and q ≥ 1. For a finite tuple U = (u1 , . . . , us ) of
elements of Fm , write
                              GU = ⟨a1 , . . . , am | u1 , . . . , us ⟩.
(1) Fix R = (r1 , . . . , rq ) ∈ Qm,q (n0 ). There is a quadratic-time algorithm for the following restricted iso-
    morphism problem. The input is a finite tuple S = (s1 , . . . , st ) of nontrivial cyclically reduced words,
    known to be irredundant and to have symmetrization satisfying C ′ (1/6); the algorithm decides whether
    GR ∼= GS . With
                                                         Xt
                                                    N=      |sj |A ,
                                                          j=1
                                                  2
    the running time of the algorithm is O(N ). The assumptions on S can be checked within the same
    O(N 2 ) time bound; an input failing it is reported as outside the restricted problem.
(2) There is a linear-time algorithm which, given tuples R ∈ Cnq and S ∈ Cnq ′ known to belong to Qm,q (n)
    and Qm,q (n′ ), respectively, decides whether GR ∼= GS . The algorithm’s running time is linear in n′′ =
              ′
    max{n, n }; the algorithm does not test the assumptions on R, S.

Proof. For part (1), return a negative answer if t ̸= q. If t = q, use Lemma 11.1 to verify nontriviality,
cyclic reduction, irredundancy, and the C ′ (1/6) condition; if this verification fails, report that the input lies
outside the promised comparison class. The first relator r1 is strictly minimal and has trivial outer stabilizer
by (Q4). For every j and ε ∈ {±1}, run the search form of Whitehead’s algorithm on
                                                      [r1 ], [sεj ].
The total cost of these fixed 2q searches is O(N 2 ) by Theorem 7.3(4).
   For each successful search, Lemma 11.2 gives a candidate Φ with a recorded Whitehead word. Condition
(Q2) and (27) give (31) for u = r1 . Lemma 11.3 computes all Φ[ri ] in O(N 2 ) time. Compare their conjugacy
classes, up to independent inversion and permutation, with those represented by the sj . Because q is fixed,
this costs at most O(N 2 ).
   A passing candidate induces an isomorphism. Conversely, if GR ∼          = GS , Theorem B(5) supplies an au-
tomorphism carrying [r1 ] to some [sεj ]. The corresponding search succeeds. Any two candidates with this
effect differ by an element of StabOut(Fm ) ([r1 ]), which is trivial; hence the candidate found by the algorithm
carries the entire relator family correctly. This proves part (1).
   For part (2), note that, since q is fixed, r∈R |r| + s∈S |s| = q(n + n′ ) ≤ 2qn′′ = O(n′′ ). To prove
                                                P             P
part (2), we first compare the common relator lengths n, n′ . If n ̸= n′ the GR ∼      ̸ GS by Theorem B(6). If
                                                                                        =
n = n′ (so that n′′ = n = n′ ), we test the fixed 2m m! relabelings, the fixed q! component permutations, the
2q inversion choices, and the required cyclic-conjugacy relations to check whether S can be obtained from R
as in Theorem B(6) and thus determine whether or not GR ∼         = GS . Theorem B(6) proves correctness of this
procedure. Since   m,  q are fixed and cyclic conjugacy   is linear-time  decidable, the total time is linear in the
input length r∈R |r| + s∈S |s| and thus linear in n′′ .
               P           P
                                                                                                                  □
                    ISOMORPHISM RIGIDITY FOR FOR GENERIC FINITELY PRESENTED GROUPS                                      41


11.2. Enumeration. The class Qm,q (n) is invariant under Γm,q,n . Indeed, (Q1) uses the invariant core; the
neighborhood U is relabeling-invariant and counting currents are unchanged by cyclic shift and inversion;
signed overlap is invariant under all operations in (25); and the class Zm is invariant under relabeling, cyclic
shift, and inversion, while tuple stabilizers conjugate. By (Q4), the action on Qm,q (n) is free.
   Put
                                          Qn = Qm,q (n),           Bn = Cnq \ Qn .
                                                                              cr
Theorem D (Asymptotic number of isomorphism types). Fix m ≥ 2 and q ≥ 1. Let Im,q (n) be the
number of group isomorphism types represented by presentations
                                        ⟨A | r1 , . . . , rq ⟩,   (r1 , . . . , rq ) ∈ Cnq .
Then
                                        cr              (2m − 1)qn
                                       Im,q (n) ∼                            (n → ∞).
                                                       2m+q m! q! nq

Proof. Proposition 10.4 gives
                               |Qn | = |Cn |q 1 + O(e−cn ) ,           |Bn | = O(|Cn |q e−cn ).
                                                          
                                                                                                                      (32)
By Lemma 10.1, every Γm,q,n -orbit in Qn has size
                                                         2m+q m! q! nq .
Theorem B(6) says that two tuples in Qn define isomorphic groups exactly when they lie in the same orbit.
Hence the number of isomorphism types represented in Qn is
                                                     |Qn |
                                                              .
                                                2m+q m! q! nq
Every isomorphism type not represented in Qn has a representative in Bn , so
                                 |Qn |          cr              |Qn |
                               m+q         q
                                             ≤ Im,q (n) ≤ m+q              + |Bn |.
                             2     m! q! n                 2     m! q! nq
                                                                              q
                                                                                 
Since exponential decay dominates n−q , the bad-set contribution is o |Cnnq| .
   Finally, (1) gives |Cn | ∼ (2m − 1)n , proving the formula.                                                          □

                                              12. Disclosure of AI use

Preparation of this paper substantially relied on chats with ChatGPT, but the author verified all the proofs
given, reviewed and edited the content as needed and takes full responsibility for the content of the paper.
